messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Feature | El Kassem et al., KONA 2021 | User’s work |
|---|---|---|
| Dosing device type | Motor-driven, vertical micro-auger dosing apparatus discharging through a funnel onto a balance/catching container; proposed as a dynamic DEM-calibration device. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004) | Open-source, 3D-printed helical-auger doser with interchangeable 1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs; doses fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Device material | Stainless-steel auger and funnel; borosilicate-glass catching container. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000008) | PLA or PETG printed housing/reservoir, with a stepper-driven auger. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Orientation | Fixed vertical auger-dosing configuration. (pqac-00000003) | Inclined from horizontal, with controlled tilt from 0° to 30°. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Outlet size | Funnel lower opening: 6 mm; funnel upper diameter: 63 mm; funnel inclination: 45°. (pqac-00000004) | Approximately 3 mm outlet. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Reservoir size | No volumetric reservoir rating reported; cylindrical container was 64 mm in diameter and 224 mm high and was loaded with 6 g. (pqac-00000004) | Interchangeable 1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Powders tested | One powder: SpheroLac 100 lactose monohydrate, described as dry, crystalline, free-flowing and non-cohesive; volume-weighted mean size D[4,3] = 115 μm. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) | Thirteen powders, including NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose and BaCl₂; planned emphasis on alloy precursors and AM feedstocks, including stainless steel. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Auger speed range | Three discrete speeds: 400, 600 and 800 rpm. (pqac-00000008) | Continuous operating range of approximately 1–30 rpm. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Tilt angle | Not varied; device remained vertical. (pqac-00000003) | Tilt is an experimental factor swept from 0° to 30° from horizontal. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Tapping mechanism | None reported. | Solenoid mechanically taps the housing; mass released by one tap is part of the fingerprint. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Measured responses | Experimental angle of repose, bulk density and steady mass-flow rate; dosing time was derived. Translational kinetic energy was a DEM-only response because it could not be measured experimentally. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) | Mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, mass freed by one tap, afterflow time constant after stopping, zero-flow increment fraction, and closed-loop dose performance over 0.05–8 g. *(User-provided context.)* |
| DEM code | LIGGGHTS-Premium 4.X; CAD in SolidWorks, meshing with Gmsh and post-processing in ParaView. (pqac-00000001) | LIGGGHTS model of the auger outlet. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Contact model | Hertz–Mindlin soft-sphere contact with normal and tangential forces and Coulomb friction. (pqac-00000001) | Hertz–Mindlin contact. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Rolling-friction model | EPSD2 elastic–plastic spring–dashpot rolling-resistance model; rolling damping torque disabled. (pqac-00000001) | Constant-directional-torque rolling-friction model. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Cohesion model | No cohesive law used in the KONA dosing calibration because SpheroLac 100 was treated as non-cohesive. The group’s companion cohesive-powder work used modified SJKR. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006) | SJKR cohesion in the current salt model; planned cohesive–frictional inference across powders. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Parameters varied | Auger speed ω = 400, 600 or 800 rpm; particle–particle static friction μs,pp = 0.3, 0.55 or 0.8; particle–wall static friction μs,pw = 0.1, 0.25 or 0.4; particle–particle rolling friction μr,pp = 0.1, 0.4 or 0.7. (pqac-00000008) | Planned inference of effective cohesion, particle–particle and particle–wall friction, moisture sensitivity and packing-related properties; operating variables include speed, tilt and tapping. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Parameters fixed | Particle and wall Young’s moduli and Poisson ratios, restitution-related properties, particle density/size representation, filling mass, gravity and numerical timestep; particle diameter was coarse-grained sixfold and the timestep was below 20% of the Rayleigh limit. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000008) | Measured particle-size distributions are intended as model inputs; the existing salt simulation reportedly used no fitted parameters. Other fixed-versus-inferred quantities remain to be specified. *(User-provided context.)* |
| DoE/calibration method | Quadratic D-optimal design followed by multivariate regression analysis, standardized effects, adjusted-response plots, Pareto charts, contour overlays and deterministic optimization in Cornerstone. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000010) | Proposed simulation-based Bayesian calibration coupled to multi-objective, multi-task Bayesian optimization of dosing-controller settings across powders. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Number of simulations | Twenty D-optimal design simulations, followed by three confirmation simulations—one each at 400, 600 and 800 rpm—for 23 reported dosing simulations in the calibration/confirmation workflow. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) | Existing model costs approximately 26–30 CPU-min per simulated revolution; the planned Bayesian campaign size is not specified. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Regression or surrogate model | Separate quadratic multivariate response surfaces for angle of repose, bulk density, mass-flow rate and normalized average translational kinetic energy; adjusted R² values were 0.975, 0.983, 0.998 and 0.986, respectively. (pqac-00000009) | Proposed probabilistic surrogates/emulators suitable for Bayesian calibration and multi-task Bayesian optimization; exact surrogate architecture is not specified. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Calibration approach | Experimental targets were placed on predicted response contours. Superimposing the angle-of-repose, density and flow-rate contours reduced a broad non-identifiable parameter field to a small intersection; Cornerstone then selected a minimum-error point. This produced point estimates, not posterior distributions. (pqac-00000010) | Planned joint likelihood over multiple dosing-fingerprint responses to infer posterior distributions for effective powder properties and quantify parameter uncertainty. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Validation method | Three new confirmation DEM runs at 400, 600 and 800 rpm compared simulated angle of repose, bulk density, mass-flow rate and dosing time with experiments. Across 12 comparisons, mean absolute deviation was reported as 0.87% and the maximum magnitude as 2.86%. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000010) | Existing salt model reproduces approximately 105 mg/rev without fitted parameters. Planned property estimates will be checked against standardized shear, flow, density, repose, particle-size and moisture tests and assessed for AM spreadability. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Validation responses held out of fitting | None in the strong predictive-validation sense: angle of repose, bulk density and mass-flow rate were calibration targets, while confirmation runs used the same response types and the same three speed levels represented in the DoE. Dosing time was compared but is algebraically related to discharged mass and flow rate. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) | Planned held-out checks include ASTM D7891 FT4 shear, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent/tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction and loss on drying. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Number of powders fingerprinted | One. (pqac-00000003) | Thirteen already dosed; intended expansion to additional alloy precursors and AM feedstocks. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Closed-loop control | No balance-feedback control reported; the balance logged discharged mass every 0.2 s. (pqac-00000004) | Analytical-balance feedback controls incremental auger motion and dosing to target mass. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Bayesian inference with uncertainty | No. The paper used deterministic regression surfaces and selected optimized parameter combinations; it did not report priors, likelihoods, posterior distributions, credible intervals or model-discrepancy terms. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000010) | Central planned contribution: simulation-based Bayesian inference with uncertainty for cohesion, friction and packing-related properties. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Multi-task optimization | Multiple responses were fitted jointly by contour overlay, but no transfer-learning or multi-task Bayesian optimization across different powders was used. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000010) | Proposed multi-objective, multi-task Bayesian optimization of controller settings across powders. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Metal AM powders | None; pharmaceutical lactose only. (pqac-00000003) | Includes gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, with planned stainless-steel and other AM-feedstock studies under inert atmosphere. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Spreadability prediction | Not studied. The stated scope was calibration and prediction of free-flowing powder behavior in auger dosing. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002) | Intended downstream prediction of powder-bed spreadability, packing uniformity and suitability for additive manufacturing. *(User-provided context.)* |
| Self-driving-lab integration | Not present; the apparatus was framed as an industrial/pharmaceutical calibration device. ### Artifact (ID artifact-03)

| Feature/claim | Present in El Kassem 2021 or citation network? | Novelty assessment for the user’s work |
|---|---|---|
| Auger doser as a DEM-calibration device | **Yes.** El Kassem et al. expressly proposed a vertical micro-auger apparatus as a dynamic calibration device. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000023) | **Not novel alone.** Frame the contribution around the richer excitation/response protocol, probabilistic inversion, multi-powder transfer, and AM application—not merely using an auger to calibrate DEM. |
| Mass-flow rate as a calibration response | **Yes.** Mass-flow rate was one of three experimental calibration targets, measured at 400, 600, and 800 rpm. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) | **Not novel alone.** Mass per revolution at low speed may be operationally distinct, but avoid claiming first use of auger throughput for DEM calibration. |
| LIGGGHTS with Hertz–Mindlin contact | **Yes.** KONA used LIGGGHTS-Premium 4.X and Hertz–Mindlin contact mechanics. (pqac-00000001) | **Not novel.** The distinctive modeling elements are the low-speed inclined outlet, SJKR cohesion, measured PSDs, and inference workflow. |
| DoE/response-surface calibration | **Yes.** KONA used a quadratic D-optimal design and multivariate regression response surfaces. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003) | **Not novel.** Bayesian emulation and uncertainty-aware sequential design can be novel relative to this deterministic quadratic-MVRA method. |
| Contour overlay to reduce parameter ambiguity | **Yes.** KONA superimposed response contours to shrink the admissible parameter region, building on the Roessler calibration lineage. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000015) | **Not novel.** Do not present joint-response identifiability as new; emphasize posterior uncertainty, model discrepancy, and information gained from each fingerprint component. |
| Joint use of multiple bulk responses | **Yes.** Angle of repose, bulk density, and mass-flow rate were jointly used in calibration; translational kinetic energy was studied but not fitted. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008) | **Not novel in general.** Novelty must lie in the particular dynamic fingerprint and cross-powder probabilistic treatment. |
| Tilt-angle sweep of an inclined auger | **Not found.** KONA used a fixed vertical configuration; no tilt sweep appears in the retrieved network. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004) | **Strong candidate novelty.** Claim cautiously as a systematic speed–inclination response surface for property-sensitive dosing, subject to a final targeted search. |
| Solenoid tapping and tap-freed mass response | **Not found** in KONA or the retrieved citation network. | **Strong candidate novelty.** Present tapping as a controlled mechanical perturbation that probes arch breakage/cohesive retention, not merely an anti-clogging accessory. |
| Afterflow time constant after auger stopping | **Not found.** KONA analyzed steady flow and total dosing time, not post-stop decay dynamics. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) | **Strong candidate novelty.** Define the fitting window and stochastic model clearly and show repeatability before interpreting it mechanistically. |
| Fraction of increments with zero flow | **Not found** in the retrieved auger-calibration literature. | **Strong candidate novelty.** This intermittent-flow statistic could be especially discriminating for cohesive powders, but should be modeled as a censored/count or Bernoulli response rather than a continuous Gaussian quantity. |
| “Dosing fingerprint” combining speed, tilt, tapping, afterflow, and intermittency | **Not found as this integrated construct.** KONA combined three conventional bulk responses but did not measure the proposed dynamic profile. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008) | **Potentially central novelty.** Define the fingerprint mathematically and demonstrate added identifiability over throughput alone through ablation or information-gain analysis. |
| Systematic fingerprints for at least 13 powders | **Not found.** KONA calibrated one free-flowing lactose powder, SpheroLac 100. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004) | **Strong scope novelty.** Avoid claiming first multi-powder DEM study generally; claim a broad, common-device dosing-fingerprint data set spanning salts, food/hydrocolloid powders, silicon, and metal feedstocks. |
| Multi-task Bayesian optimization of controller settings across powders | **Not found** in the retrieved auger/DEM network. KONA used deterministic optimization separately at each speed, not multi-task BO across powders. (pqac-00000010) | **Strong methodological novelty if implemented.** Distinguish controller optimization from Bayesian DEM calibration and specify how information transfers among powders. |
| Bayesian DEM inference with posterior uncertainty | **Present elsewhere, but not from an auger/doser in the retrieved network.** GrainLearning provides Bayesian uncertainty quantification for granular simulations; KONA reported optimized point estimates. (pqac-00000010) | **Novel combination, not a novel general method.** Claim Bayesian inference of effective powder parameters from auger fingerprints—not first Bayesian DEM calibration. |
| Held-out shear-cell and Hall/Carney-flow validation | **Not found in the retrieved auger-dosing DEM papers.** KONA confirmation reused the fitted response types and sampled speed levels rather than independent standardized tests. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) | **Strong validation novelty.** Pre-register which tests are excluded from the likelihood; call them predictive checks only if they are genuinely held out. |
| Metal-AM powders such as AlSi10Mg and stainless steel | **Not in KONA, which used pharmaceutical lactose.** The wider network contains AM-focused DEM parameterization, but not auger-response inversion. (pqac-00000003) | **Novel within this auger-inference lineage.** Do not claim novelty for DEM calibration of AM powders generally. |
| Predicting spreadability from doser-inferred properties | **Not found.** Retrieved AM work calibrates or parameterizes DEM using AM-oriented or rotating-device tests, not an auger fingerprint. | **Strong cross-operation novelty if demonstrated.** Use an actual held-out spreading experiment or recoater simulation; otherwise say “evaluate association with” rather than “predict.” |
| Open-source, 3D-printed doser | **Not found** in KONA, whose auger/funnel were stainless steel. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004) | **Practical/platform novelty.** Important for reproducibility and self-driving labs, but secondary to the scientific inference claim. |
| Integration into a self-driving laboratory | **Not found** in the retrieved DEM/doser literature; KONA framed an industrial/pharmaceutical calibration apparatus. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000026) | **Strong systems novelty.** State whether optimization is executed autonomously end to end; avoid “self-driving” if experiment selection or recovery remains manual. |
| Closed-loop balance control of dosing | **Only partially adjacent.** KONA logged balance data but did not report feedback control; Kruppa et al. used inline density/mass-flow regulation in a different commercial screw-dosing architecture. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000029) | **Novel in this specific open-source fingerprint platform, not necessarily first closed-loop powder dosing.** Soften any broad priority claim. |
| SJKR cohesion in an auger DEM calibration | **Partial precedent.** The same group’s CPM companion used modified SJKR for cohesive-powder bulk tests, whereas KONA’s auger calibration treated lactose as non-cohesive. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006) | **Potentially novel combination.** Do not claim first use of SJKR for powders; claim cohesive-parameter inference from low-speed inclined auger responses if supported. |
| No-fitted-parameter prediction of approximately 105 mg/rev for salt | **Not found** in KONA or the retrieved network; KONA fitted friction parameters to experimental targets. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) | **Notable validation result, but phrase carefully.** Specify that no parameters were adjusted to the salt throughput data, list all independently sourced inputs, and avoid implying universal parameter-free prediction. |


*Table: This table separates established auger/DEM-calibration elements from the combinations that appear distinctive in the proposed work. It also identifies where priority claims should be narrowed to avoid overlapping El Kassem’s work and broader Bayesian or AM-DEM literature.*

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting

        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available

        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.

filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Our TMS 2027 abstract is titled 'Auger-Based Powder Dosing as a Mechanistic Probe of Powder Flow Behavior: Multi-Task Bayesian Calibration and Physics-Based Property Inference'. It frames calibration of the doser as multi-objective, multi-task Bayesian optimization of controller settings across powders (mostly alloy precursors and AM feedstocks such as AlSi10Mg and stainless steel, dosed under inert atmosphere), and DEM with cohesive-frictional contact laws and measured particle-size distributions to infer effective cohesion and friction from dosing data, checked against shear-cell and Hall-flow measurements, and to anticipate spreadability and packing uniformity. A web search for that title returned: B. El Kassem, N. Salloum, T. Brinz, Y. Heider and B. Markert, 'A Semi-Automated DEM Parameter Calibration Technique of Powders Based on Different Bulk Responses Extracted from Auger Dosing Experiments', KONA Powder and Particle Journal 38 (2021) 235-250, doi:10.14356/kona.2021010. Map the citation network of that paper. (1) Summarize exactly what it did: the dosing device and its geometry, the powders, the measured bulk responses, the DEM code and contact, rolling-resistance and cohesion models, which parameters were varied and which fixed, the design of experiments, the regression models, how the contour-overlay calibration works, how many simulations, how the result was validated and what limitations the authors state. (2) Backward: which earlier works does it build on most, including the same group's auger-dosing and DEM papers (for example PAMM 2018, Journal of Drug Delivery Science and Technology 2020, Computational Particle Mechanics 2020/2021) and the DEM calibration and screw-feeder literature it relies on? (3) Forward: list as many as possible of the papers that cite it (2021 to 2026), each with full reference and DOI, and for each say what it took from the KONA paper and whether it calibrates DEM from a feeder or doser response, uses surrogate-based or Bayesian inference with uncertainty, validates on tests held out of the fit (shear cell, Hall flow, angle of repose, tapped density), covers several powders, or concerns metal additive-manufacturing powders or spreading. Group the citing papers by theme. (4) Did the same authors follow it up (for example a doctoral thesis at RWTH Aachen, later Bosch or Aachen work) by extending the method to cohesive powders, other dosing devices, or inverse identification? (5) Compare with our work as described in the context: which of our elements already appear in El Kassem et al. or in the papers that cite it, and which do not (a tilt-angle sweep of an inclined auger, solenoid tapping, multi-task Bayesian optimization of dosing controller settings, a fingerprint over 13 or more powders, Bayesian inference with uncertainty, held-out shear-cell and Hall-flow checks, metal AM powders and spreadability). Name the three papers in this network closest to our work and state, as precisely as the evidence allows, what our novelty claim should be and which claims we should drop or soften.

Abstract:
Discrete Element Method (DEM) proved to be an essential tool to optimize the industrial auger dosing process for pharmaceutical powders. During the DEM parameter calibration process of a certain powder, several parameter combinations might lead to a similar bulk response, which could also vary for other bulk responses. Therefore, a methodology is needed in order to narrow down the number of combinations and be at once close to reality representation. In this study, a vertical auger dosing setup is used as a standard calibration device to extract three different bulk responses, i.e., angle of repose, bulk density, and mass flow rate. Simulations using LIGGGHTS software package are performed based on Design of Experiments (DoE) by varying four input factors, i.e., auger speed, particle-particle and particle-wall static friction coefficients, and particle-particle rolling friction coefficient. The successful application of multivariate regression analysis (MVRA) results in predicting the bulk behavior within the studied ranges of parameters. In this regard, clustering the different predicted behaviors of the three responses together allows to dramatically reduce the admissible parameter combinations. Consequently, an optimized set of calibrated DEM parameters is chosen, where the simulation results accurately match the experimental reference data. This simple dynamic calibration tool proves to strongly verify and predict the flowability of free-flowing bulk materials.

Abstract:
One of the key challenges in the implementation of discrete element method (DEM) to model powder’s flow is the appropriate selection of material parameters, where empirical approaches are mostly applied. The aim of this study is to develop an alternative systematic numerical approach that can efficiently and accurately predict the influence of different DEM parameters on various sought macroscopic responses, where, accordingly, model validation based on experimental data is applied. Therefore, design of experiment and multivariate regression analysis, using an optimized quadratic D-optimal design model and new analysis tools, i.e., adjusted response and Pareto graphs, are applied. A special focus is laid on the impact of six DEM microscopic input parameters (i.e., coefficients of static and rolling friction, coefficient of restitution, particle size, Young’s modulus and cohesion energy density) on five macroscopic output responses (i.e., angle of repose, porosity, mass flow rate, translational kinetic energy and computation time) using angle of repose tests applied to free-flowing and cohesive powders. The underlying analyses and tests show, for instance, the substantial impact of the rolling friction coefficient and the minor role of the static friction coefficient or the particle size on the angle of repose in cohesive powders. In addition, in both powders, the porosity parameter is highly influenced by the static and rolling friction coefficients.

Abstract:
Fine‐powdered bulk materials exhibit high compressibility even under low pressure. The dosing error in volumetric dosing devices increases fundamentally with increasing product compressibility. In order to increase the dosing accuracy of a volumetric dosing of powdered bulk solids, the dosing process must be adapted to the product parameters. The most important parameter is the time‐variable product density. With a pure volumetric dosage, it has a direct influence on the actually filled product quantity. Attempts are often made to obtain feedback by means of a scale in order to continuously adjust the volume. However, this is often associated with a delay. In this article, the approach is to measure the product mass flow directly by means of a microwave sensor and to regulate it to a predetermined mass flow. The experimental investigations were carried out with a screw dosing device FVS 3111. Two scenarios were tested: on the one hand, the integration of the sensor directly at the product delivery point, whereby the difference of the average value of the dosed quantity to the target weight could be improved with the sample product coffee; on the other, the sensor was integrated directly at the beginning of the screw and the remaining product flow was simulated. A reduction of the standard deviation compared with the conventional control could also be achieved, but here, the difference between the average of the dosed quantity and the nominal quantity is greater. The cause is presumed to be the too generalized assumption of product behaviour in the case of vertical conveying by means of a screw. In summary, the dosing accuracy of a screw dosing device could be increased by measuring and regulating the mass flow and thus the costs of a manufactured packaging could be reduced.

## pqac-00000000

From text 'kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 1-2'.

Bilal El Kassem, Nizar Salloum, Thomas Brinz, Yousef Heider, and Bernd Markert. A semi-automated dem parameter calibration technique of powders based on different bulk responses extracted from auger dosing experiments. KONA Powder and Particle Journal, 38:235-250, Jan 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.14356/kona.2021010, doi:10.14356/kona.2021010. This article has 25 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies the study’s broad calibration framework but does not provide most of the detailed methodological specifications requested. The dosing apparatus is described only as a vertical auger dosing setup used as a standard calibration device; its dimensions, screw geometry, casing, inlet/outlet arrangement, and operating details are not included. The abstract refers generally to pharmaceutical powders and later to free-flowing bulk materials, but does not identify the specific powders tested. The measured bulk responses are angle of repose, bulk density, and mass flow rate. Simulations were performed with LIGGGHTS. The stated varied factors were auger speed, particle–particle static friction, particle–wall static friction, and particle–particle rolling friction. The excerpt does not specify the contact law, rolling-friction model, cohesion model, fixed parameters, DoE design or run count, regression equations, contour-overlay procedure, or validation protocol in detail. It indicates that multivariate regression analysis predicted the three responses within the studied parameter ranges, and that clustering the predicted responses narrowed admissible parameter combinations before selecting a calibrated set matching experimental reference data. No explicit limitations are stated in the supplied pages, although the method is framed as applying within studied parameter ranges and to free-flowing materials.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 5-6'.

Bilal El Kassem, Nizar Salloum, Thomas Brinz, Yousef Heider, and Bernd Markert. A semi-automated dem parameter calibration technique of powders based on different bulk responses extracted from auger dosing experiments. KONA Powder and Particle Journal, 38:235-250, Jan 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.14356/kona.2021010, doi:10.14356/kona.2021010. This article has 25 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt describes the calibration workflow and part of the DEM implementation. Experimental bulk responses from auger-dosing experiments serve as reference targets; DEM input parameters are varied according to a design-of-experiments model, followed by regression-based prediction and selection of an optimized parameter combination. Orthogonal scaling maps parameter values to [−1, 1], and a Pareto graph assesses relative parameter effects. The simulations use LIGGGHTS®-Premium 4.X, with ParaView for post-processing, SolidWorks for CAD, and Gmsh for spatial discretization. Particle contacts are modeled with Hertz–Mindlin mechanics, including normal and tangential forces, gravity, deformation, and friction. Rolling resistance uses the elastic-plastic spring-dashpot (EPSD2) model, with damping torque disabled; rolling friction is described as a correction enabling spherical particles to represent real shapes. The listed parameters include Young’s moduli, Poisson’s ratios, particle diameter, restitution coefficients, rolling-friction coefficient, wall friction/restitution settings, filling mass, particle count, timestep, and gravity. The excerpt indicates sixfold particle-size coarse-graining and a timestep below 20% of the Rayleigh critical timestep. However, it does not provide the dosing-device geometry, powder identities, cohesion model, complete varied-versus-fixed parameter assignments, DOE design, regression-model forms, contour-overlay procedure, total simulation count, validation details, or stated limitations.

## pqac-00000002

From text 'kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 12-13'.

Bilal El Kassem, Nizar Salloum, Thomas Brinz, Yousef Heider, and Bernd Markert. A semi-automated dem parameter calibration technique of powders based on different bulk responses extracted from auger dosing experiments. KONA Powder and Particle Journal, 38:235-250, Jan 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.14356/kona.2021010, doi:10.14356/kona.2021010. This article has 25 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides conclusions and validation details, but not the requested full specifications of the dosing-device geometry, powders tested, DEM code, contact law, rolling-friction model, cohesion model, or the complete list of varied and fixed parameters. The study used an auger dosing machine to obtain three reference bulk responses: angle of repose (AoR), mass flow rate (ṁ), and bulk density (BD), as functions of auger speed. The calibrated interactions included particle–particle and particle–wall static friction and particle–particle rolling friction; the excerpt specifically states that rolling friction had an overwhelmingly greater effect than particle–particle static friction. A D-optimal design of experiments and multivariate regression response models were built from only 20 simulations. Calibration used an optimization algorithm and superimposed contour plots for the three predicted responses to narrow the otherwise ambiguous set of admissible DEM parameter combinations. One optimized parameter combination was selected and experimentally validated at auger speeds of 400, 600, and 800 rpm. Across 12 validation results, the overall mean deviation was 0.87%, with a maximum deviation of 2.86% for dosing time. Stated limitations and future work include studying more material properties and bulk behaviors and extending the method from non-cohesive/free-flowing powders to cohesive powders.

## pqac-00000003

From text 'kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 2-3'.

Bilal El Kassem, Nizar Salloum, Thomas Brinz, Yousef Heider, and Bernd Markert. A semi-automated dem parameter calibration technique of powders based on different bulk responses extracted from auger dosing experiments. KONA Powder and Particle Journal, 38:235-250, Jan 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.14356/kona.2021010, doi:10.14356/kona.2021010. This article has 25 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes a vertical-oriented micro-auger dosing device used to calibrate DEM for a free-flowing pharmaceutical powder. The tested material was SpheroLac 100, a dry, non-cohesive crystalline lactose monohydrate manufactured by MEGGLE. The principal experimental bulk responses were angle of repose, mass flow rate, and bulk density; translational kinetic energy was also studied as a DEM-only response because it is difficult to measure experimentally. Simulations were performed with the open-source LIGGGHTS® code. The parametric study varied particle–particle static friction, particle–particle rolling friction, and particle–wall static friction, with auger speed also identified as a studied operating variable. The work used design of experiments, specifically a quadratic D-Optimal design, followed by multivariate regression analysis (MVRA). Calibration sought to reduce parameter ambiguity by superimposing three predicted-response contour plots to identify an approximately unique parameter combination. The excerpt states that experimental bulk behaviors were used for calibration and that the regression model was validated against those experiments. It does not provide the detailed auger geometry, contact law, rolling-friction formulation, cohesion model, fixed parameters, exact number of simulations, fitted regression equations, or detailed validation metrics; those require later sections of the article.

## pqac-00000004

From text 'kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 3-5'.

Bilal El Kassem, Nizar Salloum, Thomas Brinz, Yousef Heider, and Bernd Markert. A semi-automated dem parameter calibration technique of powders based on different bulk responses extracted from auger dosing experiments. KONA Powder and Particle Journal, 38:235-250, Jan 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.14356/kona.2021010, doi:10.14356/kona.2021010. This article has 25 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies SpheroLac 100, a dry, non-cohesive, free-flowing lactose monohydrate powder produced by MEGGLE, as the tested material. Bulk density was measured by filling 6 g into a transparent glass tube with a 24 mm inner diameter and 94 mm height. Auger dosing used a container 64 mm in diameter and 224 mm high, incorporating a stainless-steel funnel with a 63 mm upper diameter, 6 mm lower opening, and 45° inclination. The auger was motor-driven, while a balance recorded discharged mass every 0.2 s. Tests were repeated three times at 400, 600, and 800 rpm; mass flow rate and angle of repose (AoR) were measured, with AoR used as a powder cohesiveness/flowability response. The study applied a D-Optimal design with a quadratic model to investigate DEM input-parameter effects and interactions, using a 95% confidence level. Multivariate regression analysis standardized variables and used adjusted R² to assess goodness of fit; adjusted-response and Pareto graphs represented parameter effects. DEM particles were modeled as rigid bodies with translational and rotational degrees of freedom, using Newton’s equations and a soft-particle contact approach permitting small overlaps. The excerpt does not provide the DEM code, rolling-friction or cohesion models, exact varied/fixed parameters, contour-overlay calibration, simulation count, validation details, or stated limitations.

## pqac-00000005

From text 'elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 21-23'.

Bilal El-Kassem, Nizar Salloum, Thomas Brinz, Yousef Heider, and Bernd Markert. A multivariate regression parametric study on dem input parameters of free-flowing and cohesive powders with experimental data-based validation. Computational Particle Mechanics, 8:87-111, Jan 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8, doi:10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8. This article has 43 citations.

This excerpt provides only partial details relevant to the requested KONA 2021 study. The investigation covered two powders: a free-flowing powder and a cohesive powder. It examined six particle–particle DEM inputs: Young’s modulus (stiffness), particle size, particle–particle coefficient of restitution, static friction, rolling friction, and cohesion energy density. Particle–wall and wall–wall interaction properties were held constant, while particle–particle properties were varied extensively. The stated macroscopic responses included angle of repose (AoR), porosity (ε), and computational time; the excerpt also describes four macroscopic bulk responses overall, although it does not enumerate all four. A design-of-experiments approach using a quadratic D-optimal design was used to reduce the number of simulations, and regression analysis was applied to understand parameter effects and construct nonlinear prediction equations. Calibration used experimental data and a semiautomated DEM–experimental-data/regression workflow. For cohesive powder validation, a new simulation (run 54) used the experimental static-friction value and an optimized parameter combination. It predicted AoR of 40.8° versus 40° experimentally (+2% deviation), and ε of 54.84% versus 56.23% (?) as presented in the table, with −2.47% error. The excerpt does not specify dosing-device geometry, DEM software/code, contact or rolling-friction model formulations, cohesion model, contour-overlay procedure, total simulation count, or explicit study limitations.

## pqac-00000006

From text 'elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 5-6'.

Bilal El-Kassem, Nizar Salloum, Thomas Brinz, Yousef Heider, and Bernd Markert. A multivariate regression parametric study on dem input parameters of free-flowing and cohesive powders with experimental data-based validation. Computational Particle Mechanics, 8:87-111, Jan 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8, doi:10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8. This article has 43 citations.

This excerpt provides only the DEM formulation and part of the experimental characterization, not the full KONA 2021 study details requested. The particle interactions use the Hertz–Mindlin contact model, with tangential forces limited by Coulomb friction through the static friction coefficient μss. Spherical-particle shape effects are compensated using the EPSD2 rolling-resistance model implemented in LIGGGHTS; its rolling torque is bounded by the rolling coefficient μr, and damping torque is disabled. Cohesion is represented by the modified simplified JKR (SJKR) model, also implemented in LIGGGHTS. It adds a cohesive normal force Fcoh = Ca, where C is cohesion-energy density and a is contact area, making the model suitable for fine dry powders and wet or highly adhesive systems. Gravity acts in the negative z direction. Numerical stability is controlled by selecting Δt below 20% of the Rayleigh critical time. The excerpt also defines particle-shape descriptors—aspect ratio and circularity/roundness—and states that bulk density and tapped density were measured using a jolting volumeter, with five repeated measurements averaged. It does not specify dosing-device geometry, the powders tested, measured bulk-flow responses beyond BD/TD, varied versus fixed parameters, DOE, regression models, contour-overlay calibration, simulation count, validation strategy, or study limitations.

From text 'elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2'.

Bilal El-Kassem, Nizar Salloum, Thomas Brinz, Yousef Heider, and Bernd Markert. A multivariate regression parametric study on dem input parameters of free-flowing and cohesive powders with experimental data-based validation. Computational Particle Mechanics, 8:87-111, Jan 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8, doi:10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8. This article has 43 citations.

The excerpt provides only the study’s high-level scope and does not report the detailed dosing-device geometry, specific powder identities, DEM software/code, contact or rolling-friction formulations, cohesion model implementation, fixed versus varied parameter values, simulation count, detailed regression equations, contour-overlay calibration procedure, or stated limitations requested for El-Kassem et al. (KONA 2021). It does establish that the work compares free-flowing and cohesive powders using angle-of-repose experiments and DEM. Six microscopic DEM inputs were investigated: static-friction coefficient, rolling-friction coefficient, restitution coefficient, particle size, Young’s modulus, and cohesion energy density. Five macroscopic responses were examined: angle of repose, porosity, mass flow rate, translational kinetic energy, and computation time. The methodology used a design of experiments with an optimized quadratic D-optimal design, multivariate regression analysis, adjusted-response and Pareto graphs, and experimental-data-based validation. The reported findings include a substantial influence of rolling friction and a minor influence of static friction and particle size on cohesive-powder angle of repose; porosity was strongly influenced by both static and rolling friction in both powder classes. The supplied pages therefore support only a partial reconstruction of the requested methods and results.

Abstract:
<jats:p>High-fidelity models (HFMs) for twin-screw wet granulation (TSWG) are often too computationally expensiv//e for routine calibration, optimization, and digital twin deployment. This chapter presents a faster, cheaper, and easier-to-use surrogate modeling workflow that preserves HFM-level predictive capability. Sensitivity analysis is applied to prioritize influential inputs, and a rate mechanism global system analysis reduces the calibration space by 60%, leaving only 10 critical parameters. Using this reduced set, a compact mechanistic surrogate comprising 10 equations achieves accurate particle size distribution (PSD) predictions with an R of 0.998 and a simulation time of 0.41 seconds. In addition, a hybrid TSWG model is developed by coupling a population balance model (PBM) with an artificial neural network (ANN). The ANN provides rapid first-pass estimates of kinetic rate parameters within the calibration range, which are then integrated into the PBM to refine PSD predictions and accelerate calibration. The proposed workflow, adaptive framework for robust and accelerated model evaluation (AFRAME), offers a structured and efficient methodology for model calibration in continuous pharmaceutical manufacturing and supports the development of robust, adaptive digital twins applicable to a broader range of manufacturing processes.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Mechanical processes such as mixing, extrusion, and drying are key operations in food engineering, with a significant impact on product quality and process efficiency. The increasing complexity of food materials—due to non-Newtonian properties, multiphase structures, and thermal–mechanical interactions—requires advanced modeling approaches for process analysis and optimization. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) has become a vital tool in this context. This review presents recent progress in the use of CFD for simulating key mechanical operations in food processing. Applications include the analysis of fluid flow, heat and mass transfer, and mechanical stresses, supporting improvements in mixing uniformity, energy efficiency during drying, and optimization of extrusion components (e.g., shaping dies). The potential for integrating CFD with complementary models for system-wide optimization is also discussed, including challenges related to scale-up and product consistency. Current limitations are outlined, and future research directions are proposed.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The manufacturing industry, in general, and the plastic industry, in particular, have been developing new materials and process methods that need a correct study and optimization. Nowadays, the main approach to optimize these processes is using numerical methods and, in the case of particulate materials, the Discrete Elements Method to estimate the particles interactions. But those mathematical models use some parameters that depend on the material and must be calibrated, thus requiring an important computational and experimental cost. In this study, we integrate different speed-up procedures and present a general calibration method of Low-Density Polyethylene particles, to obtain the calibrated solid density and Poisson’s ratio of the material, the restitution, static and rolling friction factors in the particle-to-particle and particle-to-wall interactions, and the contact model variables (damping factor, stiffness factor, and energy density). For this calibration, four different tests were carried out, both experimentally and with simulations, obtaining the bulk density, the repose and shear angles, and the dropped powder. All these response variables were compared between simulations and experimental tests, and using genetic algorithms, the input parameters (design variables) were calibrated after 85 iterations, obtaining a Mean Absolute Percentage Error of the response variables lower than 2% compared to the experimental results.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Powder bed-based additive manufacturing processes offer an extended freedom in design and enable the processing of metals, ceramics, and polymers with a high level of relative density. The latter is a prevalent measure of process and component quality, which depends on various input variables. A key point in this context is the condition of powder beds. To enhance comprehension of their particle-level formation and facilitate process optimization, simulations based on the Discrete Element Method are increasingly employed in research. To generate qualitatively as well as quantitatively reliable simulation results, an adaptation of the contact model parameterization is necessary. However, current adaptation methods often require the implementation of models that significantly increase computational effort, therefore limiting their applicability. To counteract this obstacle, a sophisticated formula-based adaptation and evaluation method is presented in this research. Additionally, the developed method enables accelerated parameter determination with limited experimental effort. Thus, it represents an integrative component, which supports further research efforts based on the Discrete Element Method by significantly reducing the parameterization effort. The universal nature of deducting this method also allows its adaptation to similar parameterization problems and its implementation in other fields of research.

Abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Powder qualification in additive manufacturing (AM) is a complex process, requiring extensive know-how to ensure that powder properties are suitable for a specific hardware solution and AM process. This qualification is typically performed through trial-and-error methods, which are costly, time-consuming, and provide little insight into powder behavior. Without a deeper understanding of powder properties, opportunities for optimizing either the powder itself or the recoating mechanism remain unexplored. The Discrete Element Method (DEM) offers a solution by enabling virtual powder characterization and parameter optimization. A method is proposed for calibrating a DEM model of AM powder that incorporates the real particle size distribution by properly scaling the system geometry rather than relying on coarse-graining techniques. A surrogate model-based calibration approach is employed to adjust DEM model parameters simultaneously, capturing their interdependencies and combined effects. A revolution device serves as the experimental reference for the calibration process. To reduce computational costs, a scaled-down simulation setup is introduced while maintaining dimensions significantly larger than the particle size. The calibration method is demonstrated using two widely used AM powders: Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V (Ti64). The geometry down-scaling approach is validated through simulations with the calibrated model across various scaling factors. Additionally, the simulations provide insights into avalanche progression and size segregation in the revolution device. The contribution of this work is a calibration strategy for DEM-based powder modeling in AM that explicitly accounts for the real particle size distribution and is supported by validation in the revolution device. This provides a basis for reliable representation of powders in rotating drum flow, while future work should clarify the extent to which the calibrated state corresponds to the granular dynamical response during recoating.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Powder-bed-based additive manufacturing processes (PBAM) are sensitive to variations in powder feedstock characteristics, and yet the link between the powder properties and process performance is still not well established, which complicates the powder selection, quality control, and process improvement processes. An accurate assessment of the powder characteristics and behavior during recoating is important and must include the flow and packing properties of the powders, which are dependent on the application conditions. To fulfill the need for suitable powder testing techniques, a novel apparatus is developed to reproduce the generic PBAM powder spreading procedure and allow the measurements of the powder bed density, surface uniformity, and spreading forces as functions of the powder characteristics and spreading conditions, including the spreading speed and the type of spreading mechanism. This equipment could be used for research and development purposes as well as for the quality control of the PBAM powder feedstock, as showcased in this paper using a gas-atomized Ti-6Al-4V powder (D10 = 25.3 µm, D50 = 35.8 µm and D90 = 46.4 µm) spread using a rigid blade by varying the recoating speed from 100 to 500 mm/s and the layer thickness from 30 to 100 µm.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The calibration of discrete element method (DEM) simulations is typically accomplished in a trial-and-error manner. It generally lacks objectivity and is filled with uncertainties. To deal with these issues, the sequential quasi-Monte Carlo (SQMC) filter is employed as a novel approach to calibrating the DEM models of granular materials. Within the sequential Bayesian framework, the posterior probability density functions (PDFs) of micromechanical parameters, conditioned to the experimentally obtained stress–strain behavior of granular soils, are approximated by independent model trajectories. In this work, two different contact laws are employed in DEM simulations and a granular soil specimen is modeled as polydisperse packing using various numbers of spherical grains. Knowing the evolution of physical states of the material, the proposed probabilistic calibration method can recursively update the posterior PDFs in a five-dimensional parameter space based on the Bayes’ rule. Both the identified parameters and posterior PDFs are analyzed to understand the effect of grain configuration and loading conditions. Numerical predictions using parameter sets with the highest posterior probabilities agree well with the experimental results. The advantage of the SQMC filter lies in the estimation of posterior PDFs, from which the robustness of the selected contact laws, the uncertainties of the micromechanical parameters and their interactions are all analyzed. The micro–macro correlations, which are byproducts of the probabilistic calibration, are extracted to provide insights into the multiscale mechanics of dense granular materials.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Micro-scale mechanisms, such as inter-particle and particle-fluid interactions, govern the behaviour of granular systems. While particle-scale simulations provide detailed insights into these interactions, their computational cost is often prohibitive. At a recent Lorentz Center Workshop on “
                    <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://www.lorentzcenter.nl/machine-learning-for-discrete-granular-media.html" ext-link-type="uri">Machine Learning for Discrete Granular Media</jats:ext-link>
                    ”, researchers explored how machine learning approaches can aid the development of constitutive laws and efficient data-driven surrogates for granular materials while also addressing uncertainty quantification. Attended by researchers from both the granular materials (GM) and machine learning (ML) communities, the workshop brought the ML community up to date with GM challenges. This position paper emerged from the workshop discussions. In this position paper, we define granular materials and identify seven key challenges that characterise their distinctive behaviour across various scales and regimes–ranging from gas-like to fluid-like and solid-like. Addressing these challenges is essential for developing robust and efficient models for the digital twinning of granular systems in various industrial applications. To showcase the potential of ML to the GM community, we present classical and emerging machine/deep learning techniques that have been, or could be, applied to granular materials. We reviewed sequence-based learning models for path-dependent constitutive behaviour, followed by encoder-decoder type models for representing high-dimensional data in reduced spaces. We then explore graph neural networks and recent advances in neural operator learning. The latter captures the emerging field evolution of interacting particles via efficient latent space representation. Lastly, we discuss model-order reduction and probabilistic learning techniques for high-dimensional parameterised systems, both of which are crucial for quantifying and incorporating uncertainties arising from physics-based and data-driven models. We present a typical workflow aimed at unifying data structures and modelling pipelines and guiding readers through the selection, training, and deployment of ML surrogates for granular material simulations. Finally, we illustrate the workflow’s practical use with two representative examples, focusing on granular materials in solid-like and fluid-like regimes.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The discrete element method (DEM) has become an important numerical tool for investigating the interactions between agricultural machinery and granular agricultural materials. By enabling the analysis of particle-scale dynamics and macroscopic system behavior, the DEM provides valuable support for the design, optimization, and performance evaluation of agricultural equipment. This paper presents a comprehensive review of advances in the application of the DEM in agricultural machinery, with particular emphasis on material modeling, parameter calibration strategies, and the simulation of machine operational processes. First, the establishment of DEM models for major agricultural materials, including soil, seeds, and plant residues, is analyzed, highlighting commonly adopted contact models and calibration methodologies. Second, the application of the DEM in the simulation of key agricultural operations, such as soil tillage, material conveying, and harvesting processes, is examined to identify current capabilities and limitations. Finally, the main technical challenges and future research directions are discussed, focusing on improving model accuracy, validation practices, and integration with experimental and industrial workflows. Among the studies analyzed, the results showed varying performance when comparing experimental and simulated values, with the best results exhibiting a relative difference of less than 1%. However, persistent challenges regarding transferability and computational cost limit industrial-scale adoption. This review aims to provide an organized framework to guide future developments and promote the effective use of the DEM in the design and optimization of agricultural machinery.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Calibration and validation represent crucial but often-overlooked ingredients in the successful application of discrete element method (DEM) simulations. Without rigorous calibration/validation protocols, the results of DEM simulations can be imprecise or even unphysical, yet all too often the methods used by practitioners are at best cursory, and at worst entirely absent. As the particle-handling industries show an increasing interest in DEM, it is vital that this issue be resolved lest a potentially powerful tool be written off by industry as unreliable. In this work, we provide a concise overview of contemporary methods used in the calibration and validation of DEM simulations of powder flows, providing practical insights into their strengths and weaknesses, and ideas for manners in which they may be improved and/or rendered more easily adoptable in the future.

Abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cohesive contact between soil particles plays a key role in the micro‐ and macroscale responses of geomaterials, but the contact behavior can vary widely depending on different contexts. As our understanding of cohesive contact and the use of appropriate models when simulating cohesive materials is still limited, this study provides a comprehensive assessment of the most commonly used cohesive contact models, such as the Johnson–Kendall–Roberts (JKR), Simplified JKR (SJKR), Easo liquid bridge (ELB), and Derjaguin–Muller–Toporov (DMT) models. Not only are extensive reviews and analyses made to highlight crucial differences in the concept and mechanisms that different models utilize to govern cohesive bonds, but a series of 369 DEM simulations of the drawdown (DD) tests used by these models is also implemented. Cohesion and rolling friction degrees are varied in tandem, followed by detailed analyses of micro and macroscale features ranging from interparticle contact to bulk deformation characteristics across different cohesive models. The results show there are large differences in interparticle behavior depending on how the attractions are formed and developed, despite yielding similar macroscale responses. Soft bond models like ELB and DMT, whose attraction concentrates around the border of the contact region, result in weak bonds and less impact on structural features such as the contact network and porosity, especially under different dynamic contexts. This study significantly enhances understanding of different forms of cohesions and suggests criteria that can be used to select cohesive models, promoting accurate predictions of micro‐to‐macroscale responses.</jats:p>
