Abstract:
<jats:p>The initiation of the caving process in block/panel caving is critical to the success of mines. However, there is no widely adopted methodology for modeling the onset of caving. This study proposes a methodology to model the initial stages of caving using the Discrete Element Method, in which the rock mass is represented using the Bonded Particle Model, and the undercut material is modeled with non-cohesive discrete particles. The collapse of the rock mass was replicated following a parameter calibration process, and the results were compared with actual mining data of the observed initial fragmentation. Key parameters were identified, such as allowable normal and shear stresses, which are essential to accurately represent the collapse of the rock mass and the evolution of the early stage of rock fragmentation. Low allowable stress values led to premature collapse and finer fragmentation, whereas higher values delayed cave back failure and resulted in coarser initial fragmentation. The results showed the formation of large rock fragments between 14 and 15 m during the initial cave back failures. Subsequently, larger fragments ranging from 2 to 9 m were observed detaching from the cave back as draw progressed, with sizes comparable to those reported in some block/panel caving operations. The main contribution of this work is a methodology that demonstrates the feasibility of modeling caving initiation, which is crucial in a context where increasing rock mass strength and deposit depth require design changes at the production level and pose significant uncertainty in the rock mass response.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The flowability of granular bauxite materials critically affects the efficiency of industrial systems such as moving bed heat exchangers (MBHEs) in concentrated solar power (CSP) applications. This study investigates the influence of particle shape and size on flow properties using experimental methods and Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations. The static angle of repose (AoR) tests revealed higher AoR and flow resistance in non-spherical particles. Furthermore, dynamic and shear tests provided deeper insights into the flow behavior, highlighting not only shape-related effects but also a distinct sensitivity to particle size. Specifically, smaller non-spherical particles exhibited reduced interlocking and frictional resistance compared to their larger counterparts, whereas spherical particles demonstrated flow characteristics that were largely independent of size. DEM simulations were validated against experimental AoR data and accurately reflected shape-dependent behavior. The flow characteristics of cylindrical particles, which represent non-spherical shapes, exhibited a mild sensitivity to rolling friction parameters, in contrast to spherical particles, whose flow was more significantly affected by these parameters. Overall, these research results highlight the critical role of shape and size in flow behavior and provide a validated DEM framework for simulating bauxite flow, offering valuable insights for optimizing particle handling and enhancing MBHE performance in CSP systems.

Abstract:
In agricultural machinery design and optimization, the discrete element method (DEM) has played a major role due to its ability to speed up the design and manufacturing process by reducing multiple prototyping, testing, and evaluation under experimental conditions. In the field of soil dynamics, DEM has been mainly applied in the design and optimization of soil-engaging tools, especially tillage tools and furrow openers. This numerical method is able to capture the dynamic and bulk behaviour of soils and soil–tool interactions. This review focused on the various aspects of the application of DEM in the simulation of tillage and furrow opening for tool design optimization. Different contact models, particle sizes and shapes, and calibration techniques for determining input parameters for tillage and furrow opening research have been reviewed. Discrete element method predictions of furrow profiles, disturbed soil surface profiles, soil failure, loosening, disturbance parameters, reaction forces, and the various types of soils modelled with DEM have also been highlighted. This pool of information consolidates existing working approaches used in prior studies and helps to identify knowledge gaps which, if addressed, will advance the current soil dynamics modelling capability.

The excerpt is directly relevant to El Kassem’s work on auger dosing of powders using DEM simulations, but it identifies a peer-reviewed 2021 KONA journal article rather than a doctoral dissertation. The study develops a semi-automated DEM parameter-calibration method intended to address the ambiguity that occurs when multiple combinations of micromechanical parameters produce similar bulk behavior. It investigates a vertical-oriented micro-auger dosing process for free-flowing pharmaceutical lactose powder (SpheroLac 100). The principal measured or simulated bulk responses are angle of repose, mass flow rate, and bulk density; translational kinetic energy is also examined through DEM. The calibration workflow combines a parametric study, Design of Experiments (DoE), a quadratic D-optimal design, and multivariable regression analysis (MVRA). Simulations were conducted using the open-source LIGGGHTS software with parallel computing. The work studies auger speed and particle-particle static and rolling friction, together with particle-wall static friction, emphasizing that wall friction is an important parameter often omitted in prior studies. Experimental tests include bulk-density measurement in a glass tube and auger discharge measurements. The article concludes that multiple calibration tests can produce more accurate and realistic DEM results and presents the simple auger dosing machine as a potential standard calibration device for industrial applications.

Abstract:
The development of modern cutting-edge technology relies heavily on the huge success and advancement of nanotechnology, in which nanomaterials and nanostructures provide the indispensable material cornerstone. Owing to their nanoscale dimensions with possible quantum limit, nanomaterials and nanostructures possess a high surface-to-volume ratio, rich surface/interface effects, and distinct physical and chemical properties compared with their bulk counterparts, leading to the remarkably expanded horizons of their applications. Depending on their degree of spatial quantization, low-dimensional nanomaterials are generally categorized into nanoparticles (0D); nanorods, nanowires, and nanobelts (1D); and atomically thin layered materials (2D). This review article provides a comprehensive guide to low-dimensional nanomaterials and nanostructures. It begins with the classification of nanomaterials, followed by an inclusive account of nanofabrication and characterization. Both top-down and bottom-up fabrication approaches are discussed in detail. Next, various significant applications of low-dimensional nanomaterials are discussed, such as photonics, sensors, catalysis, energy storage, diverse coatings, and various bioapplications. This article would serve as a quick and facile guide for scientists and engineers working in the field of nanotechnology and nanomaterials.

Abstract:
Most nuclear safety agencies around the world agree that deep geological repositories (DGRs) constructed hundreds of meters below ground in stable host rock formations are viable solutions to safely isolate used nuclear fuel. In Canada, the DGR design involves storing used nuclear fuel in sealed copper coated used fuel containers (UFC) surrounded by highly compacted bentonite blocks (HCB) ~500 m underground. Shortly after emplacement, heat generated by radioactive decay of the used fuel will warm the UFC and its surroundings, desiccating the HCB and decreasing moisture on the container surface. As water vapour is driven from the UFC surface, the presence of minor amounts of dissolved salts may cause droplet formation prior to complete evaporation, during which deposits of salts may be left behind on the UFC. Later, as conditions evolve and the relative humidity increases and the temperature decreases, condensation of liquid water on the UFC surfaces will produce droplets again, due to the deliquescence of minor salt deposits. In either the wetting or the drying scenario, secondary spreading and spatial separation of anodic and cathodic reactions and consequent non-uniform corrosion could be possible, due to the droplet geometry.
 To investigate this scenario, the quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) technique is being used. The QCM initially consists of a quartz plate, covered by gold electrodes on both sides where a layer of copper is deposited on the crystal by using magnetron sputtering. In this technique, the change in the resonance frequency of a vibrating quartz crystal is correlated to its mass change due to the corrosion process. To investigate the effect of salts and their deliquescence behaviours, different salts (NaCl, CaCl2, and MgCl2) and CR10-E simulated groundwater were loaded on the copper surface using an inkjet printer, and then corrosion tests were performed at different temperatures and relative humidity (RH) values. In parallel, a set of long-term vapour-phase corrosion tests was performed on wrought and cold-sprayed copper coupons at 75 °C and different RH values. As part of the post-experiment analysis, the corrosion products were analyzed using a suite of surface analysis techniques, including optical microscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
 The results from QCM experiments at RH values below salts deliquescence point showed a low mass change that could correlate with less corrosion in comparison to the experiments at RH values above salts deliquescence point. It’s worth noting that even at RH values below the deliquescence point of the salts, a trace of corrosion was observed which could be indicative of the presence of monolayers of water on the surface. The results obtained from NaCl and CR10-E exposure conditions showed higher mass change and therefore higher corrosion in comparison to CaCl2 and MgCl2 salts. As for the long-term vapour-phase corrosion tests, Raman spectroscopy confirmed the presence of CuO and Cu2O on the surface as corrosion products. Further surface characterizations and mass loss measurements are underway to determine the extent of corrosion on the copper coupons.

                  <jats:p>Laboratory robotics is advancing from routine automation toward autonomous systems capable of intelligent decision-making and flexible execution. This perspective outlines key milestones and introduces the ADePT framework, which defines four core dimensions of robotic capability proficiency: adaptability and learning, dexterity, perception, and task complexity. We discuss future directions for self-driving laboratories, including robot-centric, end-to-end robotic integration, and collaborative human–robot environments. By connecting present technologies to emerging system configurations, this work offers a foundation for designing autonomous laboratory ecosystems that support scientific discovery and operational efficiency.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms possess the capability to accelerate the design of novel materials; however, their advancement in materials science is severely hindered by a fundamental deficit of experimental data, commonly referred to as data starvation. Unlike solution-based chemistry, where high-throughput (HT) technologies are a well-established standard, the automated synthesis of solid materials—particularly polymers and multicomponent composites—poses an extreme engineering challenge. Furthermore, the traditional, manual research model is inherently flawed by human bias, notably the systematic non-publication of negative results, which deprives AI models of critical boundary information regarding the design space. This paper is the first in a three-part review series defining the architecture of a fully automated, unbiased “data factory” for closed-loop discovery. This section focuses on the physical foundations of the HT workflow: experimental planning, automated synthesis, and material management. Emphasis is placed on the paradigm shift from classical, discrete Design of Experiments (DoE) to the novel concept of Continuous Gradient DoE. It reviews how robotic platforms utilizing precise gravimetric and volumetric feeders, integrated with extruders and in-line capillary rheology, enable the seamless, high-throughput manufacturing of thermoplastics and composites. Moreover, an innovative approach to sample logistics is presented, redefining classical storage patterns through the implementation of Continuous Material Management. This encompasses direct physical tagging (e.g., inkjet marking on continuous filaments or films), spool-based transport systems, and precise, real-time metadata mapping. As demonstrated, the integration of these systems yields an order-of-magnitude increase in productivity (generating tens of thousands of novel material variants annually), a radical reduction in unit costs, and the production of terabytes of standardized, machine-readable data. Establishing this reliable hardware and analytical infrastructure represents the essential first step toward unlocking the full potential of artificial intelligence in advanced materials engineering.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As photopolymer additive manufacturing matures, there is an increasing need for on-demand, application-specific materials. A major bottleneck is the limited exploration of the vast design space for new thermoset polymer formulations, which must satisfy both material property requirements and processing constraints. This challenge arises from the combinatorial complexity of formulations and the high cost of experimental evaluation. In this work, we present an end-to-end pipeline that integrates a partial self-driving laboratory (p-SDL) with informatics-driven optimization to discover and validate thermoset acrylate formulations. The pipeline begins with a thermoset acrylate database that consolidates multiple data sources, including in-house experiments, molecular dynamics simulations, and literature data. These data sets are used to train single-task and multitask predictive models, which interface directly with the p-SDL to guide experiments and measure mechanical and processing-related properties. Each component is validated independently and then deployed together to optimize a target elastomeric material with over 90% reduction in human effort. The complete optimization required only ∼40 h of active experimental time, demonstrating rapid identification of formulations that satisfy multiple target properties without exhaustive screening. This work establishes a scalable framework for embedding multifidelity machine learning within laboratory workflows, enabling autonomous, data-driven thermoset formulation discovery.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>This comprehensive review examines the evolution of autonomous materials synthesis laboratories that integrate artificial intelligence with advanced robotics to accelerate discovery. Traditional materials development pipelines typically require 10-20 years, but self-driving laboratories (SDLs) and Materials Acceleration Platforms (MAPs) aim to reduce this to 1-2 years through closed-loop systems combining physical experimentation with computational intelligence. The review analyzes critical components including robotic hardware architectures, integrated analytical instrumentation, closed-loop optimization strategies, AI-driven decision-making frameworks, and multi-agent systems for laboratory coordination. Case studies demonstrate remarkable success across various domains: nanomaterials synthesis, inorganic materials exploration, electrocatalyst discovery, and reaction mechanism elucidation. Large language models have recently enhanced these systems by improving knowledge extraction, experimental planning, and multi-agent coordination. The integration of standardized data formats, accessible materials databases, and sophisticated knowledge representation frameworks further accelerates discovery while enhancing reproducibility. This transformative paradigm represents a fundamental reimagining of materials science methodology, shifting from human-guided exploration to AI-orchestrated discovery campaigns.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The concept of self-driving chemical laboratories builds on top of two technologies: robust artificial intelligence models that translate synthesis designs into executable instructions, potentially incorporating instrument feedback, and robotic workstations capable of executing those procedures seamlessly and without human intervention. Here we present RoboRXN, a cloud-native framework that unifies transformer-based retrosynthesis and chemical action extraction or prediction models with a commercially available synthesis robot and in-line high-resolution LC–MS. Across more than 3000 actions autonomously executed, we analyzed in details 33 reactions distributed among 10 single-step reactions and 9 multi-step campaigns. Eightythree percent of single-steps and all two-step routes succeeded without parameter adjustment; a branched four-step synthesis completed after one on-deck modification. Regardless of the overall success, we systematically encountered three recurring bottlenecks: hardware rigidity, execution-level data gaps, and slow physical feedback, which are seldom reported in the literature, despite being common to many commercial platform design. We delineate how each failure surfaced, quantify its impact on yield or throughput, and outline engineering and data-centric remedies. By publishing both the successes and the blind spots, we hope to redirect community effort from one-off demonstrations toward robust, transparent, and widely adoptable AI-driven laboratories.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has catalyzed a paradigm shift in computational chemistry and materials science, evolving from passive prediction tools to active autonomous agents capable of orchestrating complex scientific workflows. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of LLM based systems in chemistry and materials science from 2020 onwards, establishing a taxonomy that progresses from domain specific language models through tool augmented systems to fully autonomous closed loop discovery platforms. We systematically examine chemical foundation models including ChemBERTa, MoLFormer, and MolT5, alongside materials-focused architecture such as MatSciBERT and MatterGPT. We evaluate their capabilities across molecular property prediction, reaction planning, materials design, and experimental optimization. The review critically analyzes agentic systems such as ChemCrow, Coscientist, and multi agent frameworks that integrate retrieval, simulation tools, and robotic laboratory interfaces to enable autonomous experimentation. Detailed benchmark mappings, evaluation metrics, and reproducibility standards are presented while addressing critical challenges in verification, safety, and trustworthiness for lab facing AI agents. Special emphasis is placed on grounding strategies to mitigate hallucinations, formal constraint validation, and human in the loop safeguards. Our analysis reveals that while current systems demonstrate impressive capabilities in constrained tasks, fundamental challenges remain in true chemical reasoning, uncertainty quantification, and long horizon planning. We conclude by outlining a research agenda for multimodal scientific foundation models, standardized community benchmarks, and governance frameworks necessary for the responsible deployment of autonomous discovery systems in chemistry and materials laboratories.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Background: Rock–blast design is a canonical inverse problem that joins elastodynamic partial differential equations (PDEs), fracture mechanics, and stochastic heterogeneity. Objective: Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) protocol, a systematic review of mathematical methods for geomechanically informed blast modelling and optimisation is provided. Methods: A Scopus–Web of Science search (2000–2025) retrieved 2415 records; semantic filtering and expert screening reduced the corpus to 97 studies. Topic modelling with Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers Topic (BERTOPIC) and bibliometrics organised them into (i) finite-element and finite–discrete element simulations, including arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian (ALE) formulations; (ii) geomechanics-enhanced empirical laws; and (iii) machine-learning surrogates and multi-objective optimisers. Results: High-fidelity simulations delimit blast-induced damage with ≤0.2 m mean absolute error; extensions of the Kuznetsov–Ram equation cut median-size mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) from 27% to 15%; Gaussian-process and ensemble learners reach a coefficient of determination (R2>0.95) while providing closed-form uncertainty; Pareto optimisers lower peak particle velocity (PPV) by up to 48% without productivity loss. Synthesis: Four themes emerge—surrogate-assisted PDE-constrained optimisation, probabilistic domain adaptation, Bayesian model fusion for digital-twin updating, and entropy-based energy metrics. Conclusions: Persisting challenges in scalable uncertainty quantification, coupled discrete–continuous fracture solvers, and rigorous fusion of physics-informed and data-driven models position blast design as a fertile test bed for advances in applied mathematics, numerical analysis, and machine-learning theory.

A semi-automated dem parameter calibration technique of powders based on different bulk responses extracted from auger dosing experiments. KONA Powder and Particle Journal, 38:235-250, Jan 2021. The excerpt is from El Kassem et al.’s 2021 KONA paper, not from the Coetzee and Scheffler 2022 review, so it does not state what that review says about either publication. It does provide the KONA paper’s own characterization of its auger-dosing calibration method. The method uses auger dosing to jointly calibrate angle of repose (AoR), mass flow rate (ṁ), and bulk density (BD), in relation to particle–particle and particle–wall static friction and particle–particle rolling friction. A design-of-experiments and multivariate regression approach used only 20 simulations, generated prediction models, and superimposed contour plots to narrow the otherwise ambiguous range of DEM parameter combinations. The selected parameter set was experimentally validated, with a maximum deviation of 2.86% and an overall mean deviation of 0.87% across the reported responses. The paper also states that particle–particle rolling friction had a stronger effect than particle–particle static friction. The excerpt lists the authors’ 2020 Computational Particle Mechanics article, titled “A Multivariate regression parametric study on DEM input parameters of free-flowing and cohesive powders with experimental data-based validation,” but provides no substantive description of that article or of the 2022 review’s assessment of it.

The excerpt does not contain the Coetzee and Scheffler (2022) review, so it cannot establish what that review specifically says about either paper. It does provide details about the cited El Kassem et al. KONA 2021 study. That work presents a semi-automated DEM calibration method for powders using a vertical auger dosing setup and three measured bulk responses: angle of repose, bulk density, and mass flow rate. LIGGGHTS simulations vary auger speed, particle–particle and particle–wall static friction, and particle–particle rolling friction within a Design of Experiments framework. Multivariate regression predicts the bulk responses, while clustering the predicted behaviors narrows the admissible parameter combinations and identifies calibrated parameters whose simulations match experimental reference data. The introduction also briefly characterizes El Kassem et al. (2020) as a systematic DoE/MVRA approach for studying how DEM input parameters affect multiple bulk responses, with reported agreement between predicted and experimental angle-of-repose and porosity data for free-flowing and cohesive powders. No bibliographic or evaluative statement from the 2022 review itself is included in this excerpt.

| Feature/claim | Present in El Kassem 2021 or citation network? | Novelty assessment for the user’s work |
|---|---|---|
| Auger doser as a DEM-calibration device | **Yes.** El Kassem et al. expressly proposed a vertical micro-auger apparatus as a dynamic calibration device. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000023) | **Not novel alone.** Frame the contribution around the richer excitation/response protocol, probabilistic inversion, multi-powder transfer, and AM application—not merely using an auger to calibrate DEM. |
| Mass-flow rate as a calibration response | **Yes.** Mass-flow rate was one of three experimental calibration targets, measured at 400, 600, and 800 rpm. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) | **Not novel alone.** Mass per revolution at low speed may be operationally distinct, but avoid claiming first use of auger throughput for DEM calibration. |
| LIGGGHTS with Hertz–Mindlin contact | **Yes.** KONA used LIGGGHTS-Premium 4.X and Hertz–Mindlin contact mechanics. (pqac-00000001) | **Not novel.** The distinctive modeling elements are the low-speed inclined outlet, SJKR cohesion, measured PSDs, and inference workflow. |
| DoE/response-surface calibration | **Yes.** KONA used a quadratic D-optimal design and multivariate regression response surfaces. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003) | **Not novel.** Bayesian emulation and uncertainty-aware sequential design can be novel relative to this deterministic quadratic-MVRA method. |
| Contour overlay to reduce parameter ambiguity | **Yes.** KONA superimposed response contours to shrink the admissible parameter region, building on the Roessler calibration lineage. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000015) | **Not novel.** Do not present joint-response identifiability as new; emphasize posterior uncertainty, model discrepancy, and information gained from each fingerprint component. |
| Joint use of multiple bulk responses | **Yes.** Angle of repose, bulk density, and mass-flow rate were jointly used in calibration; translational kinetic energy was studied but not fitted. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008) | **Not novel in general.** Novelty must lie in the particular dynamic fingerprint and cross-powder probabilistic treatment. |
| Tilt-angle sweep of an inclined auger | **Not found.** KONA used a fixed vertical configuration; no tilt sweep appears in the retrieved network. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004) | **Strong candidate novelty.** Claim cautiously as a systematic speed–inclination response surface for property-sensitive dosing, subject to a final targeted search. |
| Solenoid tapping and tap-freed mass response | **Not found** in KONA or the retrieved citation network. | **Strong candidate novelty.** Present tapping as a controlled mechanical perturbation that probes arch breakage/cohesive retention, not merely an anti-clogging accessory. |
| Afterflow time constant after auger stopping | **Not found.** KONA analyzed steady flow and total dosing time, not post-stop decay dynamics. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) | **Strong candidate novelty.** Define the fitting window and stochastic model clearly and show repeatability before interpreting it mechanistically. |
| Fraction of increments with zero flow | **Not found** in the retrieved auger-calibration literature. | **Strong candidate novelty.** This intermittent-flow statistic could be especially discriminating for cohesive powders, but should be modeled as a censored/count or Bernoulli response rather than a continuous Gaussian quantity. |
| “Dosing fingerprint” combining speed, tilt, tapping, afterflow, and intermittency | **Not found as this integrated construct.** KONA combined three conventional bulk responses but did not measure the proposed dynamic profile. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008) | **Potentially central novelty.** Define the fingerprint mathematically and demonstrate added identifiability over throughput alone through ablation or information-gain analysis. |

(pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004) | **Strong scope novelty.** Avoid claiming first multi-powder DEM study generally; claim a broad, common-device dosing-fingerprint data set spanning salts, food/hydrocolloid powders, silicon, and metal feedstocks. |

KONA used deterministic optimization separately at each speed, not multi-task BO across powders. (pqac-00000010) | **Strong methodological novelty if implemented.** Distinguish controller optimization from Bayesian DEM calibration and specify how information transfers among powders. |
| Bayesian DEM inference with posterior uncertainty | **Present elsewhere, but not from an auger/doser in the retrieved network.** GrainLearning provides Bayesian uncertainty quantification for granular simulations; KONA reported optimized point estimates. (pqac-00000010) | **Novel combination, not a novel general method.** Claim Bayesian inference of effective powder parameters from auger fingerprints—not first Bayesian DEM calibration. |

(pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) | **Strong validation novelty.** Pre-register which tests are excluded from the likelihood; call them predictive checks only if they are genuinely held out. |
| Metal-AM powders such as AlSi10Mg and stainless steel | **Not in KONA, which used pharmaceutical lactose.** The wider network contains AM-focused DEM parameterization, but not auger-response inversion. (pqac-00000003) | **Novel within this auger-inference lineage.** Do not claim novelty for DEM calibration of AM powders generally. |
| Predicting spreadability from doser-inferred properties | **Not found.** Retrieved AM work calibrates or parameterizes DEM using AM-oriented or rotating-device tests, not an auger fingerprint. | **Strong cross-operation novelty if demonstrated.** Use an actual held-out spreading experiment or recoater simulation; otherwise say “evaluate association with” rather than “predict.” |

| Integration into a self-driving laboratory | **Not found** in the retrieved DEM/doser literature; KONA framed an industrial/pharmaceutical calibration apparatus. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000026) | **Strong systems novelty.** State whether optimization is executed autonomously end to end; avoid “self-driving” if experiment selection or recovery remains manual. |
| Closed-loop balance control of dosing | **Only partially adjacent.** KONA logged balance data but did not report feedback control; Kruppa et al. used inline density/mass-flow regulation in a different commercial screw-dosing architecture. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000029) | **Novel in this specific open-source fingerprint platform, not necessarily first closed-loop powder dosing.** Soften any broad priority claim. |

(pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006) | **Potentially novel combination.** Do not claim first use of SJKR for powders; claim cohesive-parameter inference from low-speed inclined auger responses if supported. |

(pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) | **Notable validation result, but phrase carefully.** Specify that no parameters were adjusted to the salt throughput data, list all independently sourced inputs, and avoid implying universal parameter-free prediction. |

{"answer": "# Citation-Network Analysis of El Kassem et al., KONA 2021 and Comparison with the User's Auger-Dosing/DEM Program

## 1. What El Kassem et al. KONA 2021 Did

**Dosing device and geometry.** The apparatus was a vertical, motor-driven micro-auger doser designed for pharmaceutical powder filling. A cylindrical container (64 mm diameter, 224 mm height) fed powder through a stainless-steel funnel (63 mm upper diameter, 6 mm lower opening, 45° inclination) onto a borosilicate-glass catching container placed on a balance that recorded discharged mass every 0.2 s (pqac-00000004).

**Powder.** A single powder was tested: SpheroLac 100, a dry, non-cohesive, free-flowing crystalline lactose monohydrate (MEGGLE), with volume-weighted mean diameter D[4,3] = 115 μm, aspect ratio 0.746, roundness 0.891, and particle density 1.5361 g/cm³ (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000009).

**Measured bulk responses.** Three experimentally accessible responses were used for calibration: angle of repose (AoR), bulk density (BD, measured in a glass tube filled with 6 g of powder), and steady-state mass flow rate (ṁ), measured at 400, 600, and 800 rpm. A fourth response, normalized average translational kinetic energy (NA-TKE), was studied in the DEM but could not be measured experimentally (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). Experimental results were: BD = 0.758 g/cm³; ṁ = 0.2568, 0.3744, and 0.5074 g/s; AoR ≈ 33.2–33.4° (pqac-00000009).

**DEM code and contact models.** Simulations used LIGGGHTS-Premium 4.X with Hertz–Mindlin normal/tangential contact mechanics and Coulomb friction. Rolling resistance was handled by the EPSD2 (elastic–plastic spring–dashpot) model with damping torque disabled. No cohesion model was applied because the powder was treated as non-cohesive. Particle size was coarse-grained sixfold following Bierwisch et al. (2009), and the timestep was kept below 20% of the Rayleigh critical timestep. CAD was done in SolidWorks, meshing in Gmsh, and post-processing in ParaView (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006).

**Parameters varied and fixed.** Four factors were varied in a DoE: auger speed ω (400, 600, 800 rpm), particle–particle static friction μ_s,pp (0.3, 0.55, 0.8), particle–wall static friction μ_s,pw (0.1, 0.25, 0.4), and particle–particle rolling friction μ_r,pp (0.1, 0.4, 0.7). Fixed parameters included Young's moduli, Poisson ratios, restitution coefficients, particle density and scaled size, filling mass, gravity, and the numerical timestep (pqac-00000008).

**Design of experiments.** A quadratic D-optimal design required only 20 simulation runs (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008).

**Regression models.** Separate quadratic multivariate response surfaces were fitted for AoR, BD, ṁ, and NA-TKE, with adjusted R² values of 0.975, 0.983, 0.998, and 0.986, respectively. Pareto charts and adjusted-response graphs ranked parameter effects (pqac-00000009).

**Contour-overlay calibration.** For each pair of calibration parameters (μ_r,pp and μ_s,pp), predicted contour plots of the three responses were superimposed. The experimental target values defined contour lines on each surface; their intersection dramatically narrowed the admissible region. Cornerstone optimization software then selected the minimum-error parameter combination. At 800 rpm the optimized combination used μ_s,pw = 0.347 as an optimized wall-friction value (pqac-00000010).

**Number of simulations.** Twenty DoE runs plus three confirmation runs (one at each speed) totaling 23 simulations (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010).

**Validation.** Three confirmation DEM runs at 400, 600, and 800 rpm compared simulated AoR, BD, ṁ, and dosing time with experiments. Across 12 comparisons, the overall mean deviation was 0.87% and the maximum was 2.86% (for dosing time at 600 rpm) (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000010).

**Stated limitations.** The method was demonstrated only for one non-cohesive, free-flowing powder. The authors stated that future work should study more material properties and bulk behaviors and extend the method to cohesive powders (pqac-00000002). No held-out independent test types (shear cell, Hall flow, etc.) were used for validation; confirmation reused the same response types (pqac-00000010).

The following table provides a detailed feature-by-feature comparison between El Kassem et al. and the user's work:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## 2. Backward Citations: What El Kassem et al. Built On

The KONA 2021 paper draws on three distinct strands of earlier work: the same group's auger-dosing/DEM publications, the DEM calibration methodology literature, and the screw-conveyor/feeder DEM literature.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Same-group lineage.** El Kassem et al.'s PAMM 2018 paper (doi:10.1002/pamm.201800261) was the first in this sequence, using DoE to calibrate angle of repose by varying rolling friction and restitution in auger-dosing DEM simulations (pqac-00000017). The CPM 2020 paper (doi:10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8) broadened the parametric study to six DEM inputs—including cohesion energy density via the modified SJKR model—and five macroscopic responses (AoR, porosity, mass flow rate, translational kinetic energy, computation time) for both free-flowing and cohesive powders (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007). The JDDST 2020 paper (doi:10.1016/j.jddst.2020.101950) applied multivariate statistics to analyze the impact of material attributes and process parameters on auger-dosing quality, complementing the DEM-calibration strand with an experimental/statistical quality perspective.

**DEM calibration methodology.** The contour-overlay approach for resolving parameter ambiguity was pioneered by Roessler et al. (2018, Powder Technology 343, 803–812, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2018.11.034), who showed that a single bulk response permits many DEM parameter combinations and that superimposing iso-response contours from multiple tests narrows the admissible region (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000015). Coetzee's 2017 review (Powder Technology 310, 104–142, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2017.01.015) provided the broader calibration framework (pqac-00000015). Wilkinson et al. (2017, Computers & Chemical Engineering 97, 161–174, doi:10.1016/j.compchemeng.2016.11.034) used statistical sensitivity analysis to link DEM inputs to Freeman-rheometer responses, providing precedent for the MVRA methodology (pqac-00000020).

**Screw-conveyor DEM.** Owen and Cleary (2009, Powder Technology 193, 274–288, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2009.03.012; 2010, Progress in CFD 10, 327–333) established DEM prediction of screw-conveyor throughput and power (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000020). Shimizu and Cundall (2001, J. Eng. Mech. 127, 864–872) provided early 3D DEM simulations of screw conveyors (pqac-00000015). Bierwisch et al. (2009, J. Mech. Phys. Solids 57, 10–31) introduced the coarse-graining method used for particle-size scaling (pqac-00000011).

## 3. Forward Citations (2021–2026)

The KONA 2021 paper has approximately 25 citations. The following table summarizes confirmed and network-adjacent citing papers, grouped thematically, with assessment of their methodological relationship to the user's interests:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

**Theme A — DEM calibration reviews and methodology.** Coetzee & Scheffler (2022, Processes 11, 5, doi:10.3390/pr11010005) provide a comprehensive review of cohesive DEM calibration models and cite El Kassem's CPM companion (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022). Windows-Yule & Neveu (2022, Papers in Physics 14, 140010, doi:10.4279/pip.140010) review DEM calibration best practices. Irazábal et al. (2023, CPM 10, 1031–1047, doi:10.1007/s40571-022-00550-1) advance from quadratic MVRA to ML surrogates. Cheng et al. (2024, JOSS 9, 6338, doi:10.21105/joss.06338) provide the GrainLearning Bayesian uncertainty-quantification toolbox for DEM, addressing the probabilistic gap left by KONA's deterministic approach. García-Montagut et al. (2025, Polymers 17, 2748, doi:10.3390/polym17202748) develop a genetic-algorithm calibration procedure with multiple response tests for non-spherical polymer particles.

A fourth response, normalized average translational kinetic energy (NA-TKE), was studied in the DEM but could not be measured experimentally (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). Experimental results were: BD = 0.758 g/cm³; ṁ = 0.2568, 0.3744, and 0.5074 g/s; AoR ≈ 33.2–33.4° (pqac-00000009).

**DEM code and contact models.** Simulations used LIGGGHTS-Premium 4.X with Hertz–Mindlin normal/tangential contact mechanics and Coulomb friction. Particle size was coarse-grained sixfold following Bierwisch et al. (2009), and the timestep was kept below 20% of the Rayleigh critical timestep. CAD was done in SolidWorks, meshing in Gmsh, and post-processing in ParaView (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006).

**Parameters varied and fixed.** Four factors were varied in a DoE: auger speed ω (400, 600, 800 rpm), particle–particle static friction μ_s,pp (0.3, 0.55, 0.8), particle–wall static friction μ_s,pw (0.1, 0.25, 0.4), and particle–particle rolling friction μ_r,pp (0.1, 0.4, 0.7). Fixed parameters included Young's moduli, Poisson ratios, restitution coefficients, particle density and scaled size, filling mass, gravity, and the numerical timestep (pqac-00000008).

**Design of experiments.** A quadratic D-optimal design required only 20 simulation runs (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008).

# Citation-Network Analysis of El Kassem et al., KONA 2021 and Comparison with the User's Auger-Dosing/DEM Program

## 1. What El Kassem et al. KONA 2021 Did

**Dosing device and geometry.** The apparatus was a vertical, motor-driven micro-auger doser designed for pharmaceutical powder filling. A cylindrical container (64 mm diameter, 224 mm height) fed powder through a stainless-steel funnel (63 mm upper diameter, 6 mm lower opening, 45° inclination) onto a borosilicate-glass catching container placed on a balance that recorded discharged mass every 0.2 s (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 3-5).

**Powder.** A single powder was tested: SpheroLac 100, a dry, non-cohesive, free-flowing crystalline lactose monohydrate (MEGGLE), with volume-weighted mean diameter D[4,3] = 115 μm, aspect ratio 0.746, roundness 0.891, and particle density 1.5361 g/cm³ (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 3-5, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 8-10).

**Measured bulk responses.** Three experimentally accessible responses were used for calibration: angle of repose (AoR), bulk density (BD, measured in a glass tube filled with 6 g of powder), and steady-state mass flow rate (ṁ), measured at 400, 600, and 800 rpm. A fourth response, normalized average translational kinetic energy (NA-TKE), was studied in the DEM but could not be measured experimentally (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 6-8, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 8-10). Experimental results were: BD = 0.758 g/cm³; ṁ = 0.2568, 0.3744, and 0.5074 g/s; AoR ≈ 33.2–33.4° (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 8-10).

**DEM code and contact models.** Simulations used LIGGGHTS-Premium 4.X with Hertz–Mindlin normal/tangential contact mechanics and Coulomb friction. Rolling resistance was handled by the EPSD2 (elastic–plastic spring–dashpot) model with damping torque disabled. No cohesion model was applied because the powder was treated as non-cohesive. Particle size was coarse-grained sixfold following Bierwisch et al. (2009), and the timestep was kept below 20% of the Rayleigh critical timestep. CAD was done in SolidWorks, meshing in Gmsh, and post-processing in ParaView (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 5-6, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 5-6).

**Parameters varied and fixed.** Four factors were varied in a DoE: auger speed ω (400, 600, 800 rpm), particle–particle static friction μ_s,pp (0.3, 0.55, 0.8), particle–wall static friction μ_s,pw (0.1, 0.25, 0.4), and particle–particle rolling friction μ_r,pp (0.1, 0.4, 0.7). Fixed parameters included Young's moduli, Poisson ratios, restitution coefficients, particle density and scaled size, filling mass, gravity, and the numerical timestep (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 6-8).

**Design of experiments.** A quadratic D-optimal design required only 20 simulation runs (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 12-13, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 6-8).

**Regression models.** Separate quadratic multivariate response surfaces were fitted for AoR, BD, ṁ, and NA-TKE, with adjusted R² values of 0.975, 0.983, 0.998, and 0.986, respectively. Pareto charts and adjusted-response graphs ranked parameter effects (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 8-10).

**Contour-overlay calibration.** For each pair of calibration parameters (μ_r,pp and μ_s,pp), predicted contour plots of the three responses were superimposed. The experimental target values defined contour lines on each surface; their intersection dramatically narrowed the admissible region. Cornerstone optimization software then selected the minimum-error parameter combination. At 800 rpm the optimized combination used μ_s,pw = 0.347 as an optimized wall-friction value (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 10-12).

**Number of simulations.** Twenty DoE runs plus three confirmation runs (one at each speed) totaling 23 simulations (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 6-8, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 10-12).

**Validation.** Three confirmation DEM runs at 400, 600, and 800 rpm compared simulated AoR, BD, ṁ, and dosing time with experiments. Across 12 comparisons, the overall mean deviation was 0.87% and the maximum was 2.86% (for dosing time at 600 rpm) (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 12-13, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 10-12).

**Stated limitations.** The method was demonstrated only for one non-cohesive, free-flowing powder. The authors stated that future work should study more material properties and bulk behaviors and extend the method to cohesive powders (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 12-13). No held-out independent test types (shear cell, Hall flow, etc.) were used for validation; confirmation reused the same response types (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 10-12).

**DEM calibration methodology.** The contour-overlay approach for resolving parameter ambiguity was pioneered by Roessler et al. (2018, Powder Technology 343, 803–812, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2018.11.034), who showed that a single bulk response permits many DEM parameter combinations and that superimposing iso-response contours from multiple tests narrows the admissible region (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 10-12, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 13-14). Coetzee's 2017 review (Powder Technology 310, 104–142, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2017.01.015) provided the broader calibration framework (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 13-14). Wilkinson et al. (2017, Computers & Chemical Engineering 97, 161–174, doi:10.1016/j.compchemeng.2016.11.034) used statistical sensitivity analysis to link DEM inputs to Freeman-rheometer responses, providing precedent for the MVRA methodology (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 14-16).

**Screw-conveyor DEM.** Owen and Cleary (2009, Powder Technology 193, 274–288, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2009.03.012; 2010, Progress in CFD 10, 327–333) established DEM prediction of screw-conveyor throughput and power (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 13-14, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 14-16). Shimizu and Cundall (2001, J. Eng. Mech. 127, 864–872) provided early 3D DEM simulations of screw conveyors (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 13-14). Bierwisch et al. (2009, J. Mech. Phys. ## 4. Follow-Up by the Same Authors

Bilal El Kassem was a PhD candidate at Robert Bosch Packaging Technology GmbH in Stuttgart, supervised by Prof. Bernd Markert at the Institute of General Mechanics, RWTH Aachen University (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 14-16). The doctoral thesis is titled *"Machine design for auger dosing of powders by utilizing DEM simulations and analysis"* (RWTH Aachen University, 2021) and is explicitly cited by Kruppa et al. (2022) (kruppa2022increasingthedosing pages 1-11).

The publication sequence progressed as follows: (1) PAMM 2018 introduced auger-dosing DEM with DoE for AoR calibration; (2) JDDST 2020 (doi:10.1016/j.jddst.2020.101950) applied multivariate statistics to auger-dosing quality; (3) CPM 2020 (doi:10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8) extended the MVRA framework to cohesive powders using the SJKR cohesion model, examining six DEM inputs and five responses including porosity (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 21-23, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 5-6, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2); (4) KONA 2021 narrowed the method to a single-powder, multi-response auger calibration; and (5) the vertical loss-in-weight feeder prototype (doi:10.1080/10837450.2021.1901915) extended the device-design strand to gravimetric feeding.

The CPM 2020 paper is the most relevant extension to cohesive powders: it used SJKR cohesion energy density as a varied input alongside static and rolling friction, restitution, Young's modulus, and particle size, applied to angle-of-repose tests rather than to the auger-dosing setup itself (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 21-23, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 5-6). The doctoral thesis presumably consolidated these strands but was not accessible for full review.

No further publications by El Kassem, Salloum, Brinz, Heider, or Markert extending the auger-based DEM calibration to inverse identification, Bayesian inference, AM powders, or additional dosing devices were found in the retrieved literature.

**Powder.** A single powder was tested: SpheroLac 100, a dry, non-cohesive, free-flowing crystalline lactose monohydrate (MEGGLE), with volume-weighted mean diameter D[4,3] = 115 μm, aspect ratio 0.746, roundness 0.891, and particle density 1.5361 g/cm³ (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000009).

**Measured bulk responses.** Three experimentally accessible responses were used for calibration: angle of repose (AoR), bulk density (BD, measured in a glass tube filled with 6 g of powder), and steady-state mass flow rate (ṁ), measured at 400, 600, and 800 rpm. A fourth response, normalized average translational kinetic energy (NA-TKE), was studied in the DEM but could not be measured experimentally (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). Experimental results were: BD = 0.758 g/cm³; ṁ = 0.2568, 0.3744, and 0.5074 g/s; AoR ≈ 33.2–33.4° (pqac-00000009).

**DEM code and contact models.** Simulations used LIGGGHTS-Premium 4.X with Hertz–Mindlin normal/tangential contact mechanics and Coulomb friction. Rolling resistance was handled by the EPSD2 (elastic–plastic spring–dashpot) model with damping torque disabled. No cohesion model was applied because the powder was treated as non-cohesive. Particle size was coarse-grained sixfold following Bierwisch et al. (2009), and the timestep was kept below 20% of the Rayleigh critical timestep. CAD was done in SolidWorks, meshing in Gmsh, and post-processing in ParaView (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006).

**Parameters varied and fixed.** Four factors were varied in a DoE: auger speed ω (400, 600, 800 rpm), particle–particle static friction μ_s,pp (0.3, 0.55, 0.8), particle–wall static friction μ_s,pw (0.1, 0.25, 0.4), and particle–particle rolling friction μ_r,pp (0.1, 0.4, 0.7). Fixed parameters included Young's moduli, Poisson ratios, restitution coefficients, particle density and scaled size, filling mass, gravity, and the numerical timestep (pqac-00000008).

**Design of experiments.** A quadratic D-optimal design required only 20 simulation runs (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008).

**Regression models.** Separate quadratic multivariate response surfaces were fitted for AoR, BD, ṁ, and NA-TKE, with adjusted R² values of 0.975, 0.983, 0.998, and 0.986, respectively. Pareto charts and adjusted-response graphs ranked parameter effects (pqac-00000009).

**Contour-overlay calibration.** For each pair of calibration parameters (μ_r,pp and μ_s,pp), predicted contour plots of the three responses were superimposed. The experimental target values defined contour lines on each surface; their intersection dramatically narrowed the admissible region. Cornerstone optimization software then selected the minimum-error parameter combination. At 800 rpm the optimized combination used μ_s,pw = 0.347 as an optimized wall-friction value (pqac-00000010).

**Number of simulations.** Twenty DoE runs plus three confirmation runs (one at each speed) totaling 23 simulations (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010).

The authors stated that future work should study more material properties and bulk behaviors and extend the method to cohesive powders (pqac-00000002). **Same-group lineage.** El Kassem et al.'s PAMM 2018 paper (doi:10.1002/pamm.201800261) was the first in this sequence, using DoE to calibrate angle of repose by varying rolling friction and restitution in auger-dosing DEM simulations (pqac-00000017). The CPM 2020 paper (doi:10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8) broadened the parametric study to six DEM inputs—including cohesion energy density via the modified SJKR model—and five macroscopic responses (AoR, porosity, mass flow rate, translational kinetic energy, computation time) for both free-flowing and cohesive powders (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007). The JDDST 2020 paper (doi:10.1016/j.jddst.2020.101950) applied multivariate statistics to analyze the impact of material attributes and process parameters on auger-dosing quality, complementing the DEM-calibration strand with an experimental/statistical quality perspective.

**DEM calibration methodology.** The contour-overlay approach for resolving parameter ambiguity was pioneered by Roessler et al. (2018, Powder Technology 343, 803–812, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2018.11.034), who showed that a single bulk response permits many DEM parameter combinations and that superimposing iso-response contours from multiple tests narrows the admissible region (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000015). Coetzee's 2017 review (Powder Technology 310, 104–142, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2017.01.015) provided the broader calibration framework (pqac-00000015). Wilkinson et al. (2017, Computers & Chemical Engineering 97, 161–174, doi:10.1016/j.compchemeng.2016.11.034) used statistical sensitivity analysis to link DEM inputs to Freeman-rheometer responses, providing precedent for the MVRA methodology (pqac-00000020).

**Screw-conveyor DEM.** Owen and Cleary (2009, Powder Technology 193, 274–288, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2009.03.012; 2010, Progress in CFD 10, 327–333) established DEM prediction of screw-conveyor throughput and power (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000020). Shimizu and Cundall (2001, J. Eng. Mech. 127, 864–872) provided early 3D DEM simulations of screw conveyors (pqac-00000015). Bierwisch et al. (2009, J. Mech. Phys. Solids 57, 10–31) introduced the coarse-graining method used for particle-size scaling (pqac-00000011).

## 4. Follow-Up by the Same Authors

Bilal El Kassem was a PhD candidate at Robert Bosch Packaging Technology GmbH in Stuttgart, supervised by Prof. Bernd Markert at the Institute of General Mechanics, RWTH Aachen University (pqac-00000026). The doctoral thesis is titled *"Machine design for auger dosing of powders by utilizing DEM simulations and analysis"* (RWTH Aachen University, 2021) and is explicitly cited by Kruppa et al. (2022) (pqac-00000029).

The publication sequence progressed as follows: (1) PAMM 2018 introduced auger-dosing DEM with DoE for AoR calibration; (2) JDDST 2020 (doi:10.1016/j.jddst.2020.101950) applied multivariate statistics to auger-dosing quality; (3) CPM 2020 (doi:10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8) extended the MVRA framework to cohesive powders using the SJKR cohesion model, examining six DEM inputs and five responses including porosity (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007); (4) KONA 2021 narrowed the method to a single-powder, multi-response auger calibration; and (5) the vertical loss-in-weight feeder prototype (doi:10.1080/10837450.2021.1901915) extended the device-design strand to gravimetric feeding.

The CPM 2020 paper is the most relevant extension to cohesive powders: it used SJKR cohesion energy density as a varied input alongside static and rolling friction, restitution, Young's modulus, and particle size, applied to angle-of-repose tests rather than to the auger-dosing setup itself (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). The doctoral thesis presumably consolidated these strands but was not accessible for full review.

No further publications by El Kassem, Salloum, Brinz, Heider, or Markert extending the auger-based DEM calibration to inverse identification, Bayesian inference, AM powders, or additional dosing devices were found in the retrieved literature.

### Three Closest Papers

1. **El Kassem et al., KONA 2021** — The single most directly comparable work: same concept of using an auger doser as a DEM calibration device with multiple bulk responses, LIGGGHTS Hertz–Mindlin contact, DoE, and regression-based identification. It differs from the user's work in orientation (vertical vs. inclinable), scope (one non-cohesive powder vs. 13 powders), calibration method (deterministic contour overlay vs. Bayesian inference), validation (self-consistent confirmation vs. held-out standard tests), and application domain (pharmaceutical vs. metal AM).

2. **El-Kassem et al., CPM 2020** — Extends the same group's approach to cohesive powders with SJKR cohesion energy density, six DEM inputs, and five responses. It demonstrates that the MVRA/DoE methodology can accommodate cohesion, but it uses angle-of-repose bench tests rather than auger-dosing responses, and it still produces point-estimate calibrations without uncertainty quantification.

3. **Sani et al., Progress in Additive Manufacturing 2026** — The closest work in the AM domain: calibrates DEM for Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V powders using surrogate models applied to rotating-drum responses with real particle-size distributions, geometry scaling, and two powders. It addresses AM spreadability motivation and uses a surrogate-based approach, but the calibration device is a rotating drum (not an auger), no Bayesian uncertainty is reported, and no held-out standard-test validation is performed.

### Novelty Claims to Make

The user's work can defensibly claim the following novelties relative to this citation network:

1. **A richer dosing-fingerprint excitation/response protocol** comprising speed-dependent mass-per-revolution at multiple tilt angles (0–30°), solenoid-tapped mass release, afterflow time constant, and zero-flow increment fraction — none of which appear in El Kassem or any retrieved citing work.

2. **Bayesian inference of effective powder properties from auger-dosing responses with posterior uncertainty**, as opposed to deterministic contour-overlay or optimization-based point estimates. While Bayesian DEM calibration exists (Cheng et al., GrainLearning), it has not been applied to an auger or screw-feeder response in the retrieved literature.

3. **Systematic fingerprinting of ≥13 chemically and morphologically diverse powders** on a single common device, spanning salts, food hydrocolloids, silicon, and gas-atomized metal alloy precursors, compared to El Kassem's single-powder demonstration.

4. **Held-out predictive validation** of doser-inferred effective properties against independent standardized tests (FT4 shear, Schulze ring shear, Hall/Carney flow, apparent/tap density, angle of repose, sieving, laser diffraction, loss on drying) — a validation design not found in any retrieved auger-DEM calibration study.

5. **Linkage from doser-inferred properties to AM spreadability and packing uniformity**, bridging the dosing-characterization and powder-bed-spreading literatures that currently operate in isolation.

6. **Integration into a self-driving laboratory** for alloy discovery, using an open-source, 3D-printed doser under closed-loop balance control with multi-task Bayesian optimization across powders.

### Claims to Drop or Soften

- **Do not claim** to be the first to use an auger doser as a DEM calibration device — El Kassem et al. (KONA 2021) explicitly proposed this (pqac-00000023).
- **Soften** any claim of first use of multiple bulk responses for DEM calibration — Roessler et al. (2018) and El Kassem et al. (2021) both demonstrated multi-response contour overlays (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000015).
- **Soften** any claim of first Bayesian DEM calibration — Cheng et al. (2018, 2024) established Bayesian DEM inference; the user's novelty is applying it to auger-dosing fingerprints for property inference.
- **Soften** any claim of first closed-loop powder dosing — Kruppa et al. (2022) demonstrated inline density-regulated screw dosing (pqac-00000029); the novelty is the specific open-source platform and the use of dosing dynamics as a mechanistic probe.
- **Do not claim** first DEM calibration for AM powders — Girnth et al. (2024), Sani et al. (2026), Meier et al. (2019), and others have parameterized DEM for AM feedstocks. The novelty is inferring AM-relevant properties from auger-dosing fingerprints and predicting spreadability from those inferred properties.
- **Soften** the claim of a parameter-free DEM prediction (105 mg/rev for salt) — specify all independently sourced inputs and clarify that this applies to one specific non-cohesive powder configuration; do not imply general parameter-free predictability.

In summary, the user's strongest novelty claim lies in the *combination* of (a) the enriched dosing-fingerprint protocol with tilt, tapping, afterflow, and intermittency responses, (b) Bayesian inverse inference with uncertainty quantification applied to that fingerprint, (c) systematic fingerprinting across a broad set of powders including metal AM feedstocks, (d) held-out validation against standard powder-characterization tests, and (e) downstream prediction of AM-relevant spreadability — none of which has been demonstrated as an integrated package in the existing auger-dosing DEM literature.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides conclusions and validation details, but not the requested full specifications of the dosing-device geometry, powders tested, DEM code, contact law, rolling-friction model, cohesion model, or the complete list of varied and fixed parameters. The study used an auger dosing machine to obtain three reference bulk responses: angle of repose (AoR), mass flow rate (ṁ), and bulk density (BD), as functions of auger speed. The calibrated interactions included particle–particle and particle–wall static friction and particle–particle rolling friction; the excerpt specifically states that rolling friction had an overwhelmingly greater effect than particle–particle static friction. A D-optimal design of experiments and multivariate regression response models were built from only 20 simulations. Calibration used an optimization algorithm and superimposed contour plots for the three predicted responses to narrow the otherwise ambiguous set of admissible DEM parameter combinations. One optimized parameter combination was selected and experimentally validated at auger speeds of 400, 600, and 800 rpm. Across 12 validation results, the overall mean deviation was 0.87%, with a maximum deviation of 2.86% for dosing time. Stated limitations and future work include studying more material properties and bulk behaviors and extending the method from non-cohesive/free-flowing powders to cohesive powders.

contexts.context: El Kassem et al.’s DEM study used spherical SpheroLac 100 particles, six-times coarse-grained, in a CAD auger/funnel discretized with Gmsh and simulated in LIGGGHTS. A 20-run three-level DoE varied auger speed (400/600/800 rpm), particle–particle static friction (0.3/0.55/0.8), particle–wall static friction (0.1/0.25/0.4), and particle–particle rolling friction (0.1/0.4/0.7); other properties were fixed. Responses were angle of repose (AoR), bulk density (BD), mass flow rate, and normalized translational kinetic energy. Experiments measured BD = 0.758 g/cm³ and flow rates 0.2568, 0.3744, and 0.5074 g/s.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Our TMS 2027 abstract is titled 'Auger-Based Powder Dosing as a Mechanistic Probe of Powder Flow Behavior: Multi-Task Bayesian Calibration and Physics-Based Property Inference'. It frames calibration of the doser as multi-objective, multi-task Bayesian optimization of controller settings across powders (mostly alloy precursors and AM feedstocks such as AlSi10Mg and stainless steel, dosed under inert atmosphere), and DEM with cohesive-frictional contact laws and measured particle-size distributions to infer effective cohesion and friction from dosing data, checked against shear-cell and Hall-flow measurements, and to anticipate spreadability and packing uniformity. contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. contexts.context: The excerpt is directly relevant to El Kassem’s work on auger dosing of powders using DEM simulations, but it identifies a peer-reviewed 2021 KONA journal article rather than a doctoral dissertation. The study develops a semi-automated DEM parameter-calibration method intended to address the ambiguity that occurs when multiple combinations of micromechanical parameters produce similar bulk behavior. It investigates a vertical-oriented micro-auger dosing process for free-flowing pharmaceutical lactose powder (SpheroLac 100). The principal measured or simulated bulk responses are angle of repose, mass flow rate, and bulk density; translational kinetic energy is also examined through DEM. The calibration workflow combines a parametric study, Design of Experiments (DoE), a quadratic D-optimal design, and multivariable regression analysis (MVRA). Simulations were conducted using the open-source LIGGGHTS software with parallel computing. The work studies auger speed and particle-particle static and rolling friction, together with particle-wall static friction, emphasizing that wall friction is an important parameter often omitted in prior studies. Experimental tests include bulk-density measurement in a glass tube and auger discharge measurements. The article concludes that multiple calibration tests can produce more accurate and realistic DEM results and presents the simple auger dosing machine as a potential standard calibration device for industrial applications.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns a 2021 peer-reviewed KONA Powder and Particle Journal article by Bilal El Kassem, Nizar Salloum, Thomas Brinz, Yousef Heider, and Bernd Markert, rather than directly identifying an RWTH Aachen doctoral dissertation. Its subject is DEM simulation and calibration of powders in an auger-dosing process. The authors establish a semi-automated calibration method for non-cohesive powders using three measured bulk responses: angle of repose (AoR), bulk density (BD), and mass flow rate (ṁ), evaluated in relation to auger speed. Their methodology combines a D-optimal design, multivariate regression response analysis (MVRA), contour-plot superposition, and optimization to reduce ambiguity among DEM parameter combinations. The study used only 20 simulations and experimentally validated an optimized parameter set. Across 12 validation results, the maximum deviation was 2.86% and the overall mean deviation was 0.87%. The conclusions state that individual calibration tests are insufficient because multiple DEM parameter combinations can produce similar bulk responses; the particle-particle rolling friction coefficient had a stronger effect than particle-particle static friction. contexts.context: The excerpt is not a doctoral dissertation or thesis; it is a 2021 peer-reviewed KONA Powder and Particle Journal article by Bilal El Kassem and coauthors, including an affiliation with the Institute of General Mechanics at RWTH Aachen University. It is directly relevant to machine design and auger dosing of powders using DEM simulations. The study develops a semi-automated calibration method for pharmaceutical and other free-flowing powders in a vertical auger dosing setup. DEM simulations are conducted with LIGGGHTS, using Design of Experiments to vary auger speed, particle–particle and particle–wall static friction coefficients, and particle–particle rolling friction. Three experimental bulk responses—angle of repose, bulk density, and mass flow rate—are used to evaluate and calibrate the simulations. Multivariate regression analysis predicts bulk behavior over the investigated parameter ranges, while clustering the predicted responses reduces the number of admissible parameter combinations. The method selects calibrated DEM parameters whose simulated responses match experimental reference data, supporting verification and prediction of powder flowability. The excerpt also identifies the broader engineering motivation: improper screw-feeder design can cause surging, unsteady flow, inaccurate metering, segregation, excessive wear, power consumption, and start-up torque. contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Our TMS 2027 abstract is titled 'Auger-Based Powder Dosing as a Mechanistic Probe of Powder Flow Behavior: Multi-Task Bayesian Calibration and Physics-Based Property Inference'. It frames calibration of the doser as multi-objective, multi-task Bayesian optimization of controller settings across powders (mostly alloy precursors and AM feedstocks such as AlSi10Mg and stainless steel, dosed under inert atmosphere), and DEM with cohesive-frictional contact laws and measured particle-size distributions to infer effective cohesion and friction from dosing data, checked against shear-cell and Hall-flow measurements, and to anticipate spreadability and packing uniformity. Markert, 'A Semi-Automated DEM Parameter Calibration Technique of Powders Based on Different Bulk Responses Extracted from Auger Dosing Experiments', KONA Powder and Particle Journal 38 (2021) 235-250, doi:10.14356/kona.2021010. (2) Backward: which earlier works does it build on most, including the same group's auger-dosing and DEM papers (for example PAMM 2018, Journal of Drug Delivery Science and Technology 2020, Computational Particle Mechanics 2020/2021) and the DEM calibration and screw-feeder literature it relies on?
