snippets: A Semi-Automated DEM Parameter Calibration Technique of Powders Based on Different Bulk Responses Extracted from Auger Dosing Experiments
a vertical auger dosing setup is used as a standard calibration device to extract three different bulk responses, i.e., angle of repose, bulk density, and mass flow rate
Simulations using LIGGGHTS software package are performed based on Design of Experiments (DoE)
clustering the different predicted behaviors of the three responses together allows to dramatically reduce the admissible parameter combinations

El Kassem et al., 2020 developed a systematic numerical approach, using DoE and multivariate regression analysis (MVRA), to efficiently study the influence of different DEM input parameters on various bulk responses

contexts.context: A 2023 *Processes* study calibrated cohesive DEM parameters using three experiments: vertical-displacement angle of repose, rotating drum, and a newly designed centrifuge. Pull-off force \(F_0\) and distance \(D_0\) were varied factorially; contour-response overlays identified unique values for each sand grade, moisture level, and particle-scale factor. Medium/coarse sands calibrated best with angle-of-repose, drawdown, and drum tests; fine cohesive sand with angle-of-repose plus centrifuge. The centrifuge supplied many angle-versus-acceleration data points, used little material, avoided uncertain wall properties, and simulated faster. It also compares computational costs of SJKR, JKR, EEPA, and related contact models.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Our TMS 2027 abstract is titled 'Auger-Based Powder Dosing as a Mechanistic Probe of Powder Flow Behavior: Multi-Task Bayesian Calibration and Physics-Based Property Inference'. It frames calibration of the doser as multi-objective, multi-task Bayesian optimization of controller settings across powders (mostly alloy precursors and AM feedstocks such as AlSi10Mg and stainless steel, dosed under inert atmosphere), and DEM with cohesive-frictional contact laws and measured particle-size distributions to infer effective cohesion and friction from dosing data, checked against shear-cell and Hall-flow measurements, and to anticipate spreadability and packing uniformity. A web search for that title returned: B. El Kassem, N. Salloum, T. Brinz, Y. Heider and B. Markert, 'A Semi-Automated DEM Parameter Calibration Technique of Powders Based on Different Bulk Responses Extracted from Auger Dosing Experiments', KONA Powder and Particle Journal 38 (2021) 235-250, doi:10.14356/kona.2021010. Map the citation network of that paper. (1) Summarize exactly what it did: the dosing device and its geometry, the powders, the measured bulk responses, the DEM code and contact, rolling-resistance and cohesion models, which parameters were varied and which fixed, the design of experiments, the regression models, how the contour-overlay calibration works, how many simulations, how the result was validated and what limitations the authors state. (2) Backward: which earlier works does it build on most, including the same group's auger-dosing and DEM papers (for example PAMM 2018, Journal of Drug Delivery Science and Technology 2020, Computational Particle Mechanics 2020/2021) and the DEM calibration and screw-feeder literature it relies on? (3) Forward: list as many as possible of the papers that cite it (2021 to 2026), each with full reference and DOI, and for each say what it took from the KONA paper and whether it calibrates DEM from a feeder or doser response, uses surrogate-based or Bayesian inference with uncertainty, validates on tests held out of the fit (shear cell, Hall flow, angle of repose, tapped density), covers several powders, or concerns metal additive-manufacturing powders or spreading. Group the citing papers by theme. (4) Did the same authors follow it up (for example a doctoral thesis at RWTH Aachen, later Bosch or Aachen work) by extending the method to cohesive powders, other dosing devices, or inverse identification? (5) Compare with our work as described in the context: which of our elements already appear in El Kassem et al. or in the papers that cite it, and which do not (a tilt-angle sweep of an inclined auger, solenoid tapping, multi-task Bayesian optimization of dosing controller settings, a fingerprint over 13 or more powders, Bayesian inference with uncertainty, held-out shear-cell and Hall-flow checks, metal AM powders and spreadability). Name the three papers in this network closest to our work and state, as precisely as the evidence allows, what our novelty claim should be and which claims we should drop or soften.

contexts.context: The excerpt is a 2023 review of DEM calibration tests. It notes studies identifying interactions between rolling resistance and JKR cohesion (Doan et al.; Li et al.) and calibrating cohesive parameters with lifting-cylinder tests (Yu et al.; Nasr-Eddine et al.). The lifting-cylinder test is simple and scale-invariant at slow speed, but unsuitable for highly cohesive powders, which form steep, moisture-insensitive piles. A ledge/free-flow test measures four angles and two adhering masses reflecting particle–particle and particle–wall contacts; it has been modeled with SJKR-E, though physical calibration was not demonstrated for wet iron ore. Related iron-ore studies used hybrid liquid-bridge/SJKR-E or EEPA models.

# Citation-Network Analysis of El Kassem et al., KONA 2021 and Comparison with the User's Auger-Dosing/DEM Program

## 1. What El Kassem et al. KONA 2021 Did

**Dosing device and geometry.** The apparatus was a vertical, motor-driven micro-auger doser designed for pharmaceutical powder filling. A cylindrical container (64 mm diameter, 224 mm height) fed powder through a stainless-steel funnel (63 mm upper diameter, 6 mm lower opening, 45° inclination) onto a borosilicate-glass catching container placed on a balance that recorded discharged mass every 0.2 s (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 3-5).

**Powder.** A single powder was tested: SpheroLac 100, a dry, non-cohesive, free-flowing crystalline lactose monohydrate (MEGGLE), with volume-weighted mean diameter D[4,3] = 115 μm, aspect ratio 0.746, roundness 0.891, and particle density 1.5361 g/cm³ (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 3-5, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 8-10).

**Measured bulk responses.** Three experimentally accessible responses were used for calibration: angle of repose (AoR), bulk density (BD, measured in a glass tube filled with 6 g of powder), and steady-state mass flow rate (ṁ), measured at 400, 600, and 800 rpm. A fourth response, normalized average translational kinetic energy (NA-TKE), was studied in the DEM but could not be measured experimentally (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 6-8, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 8-10). Experimental results were: BD = 0.758 g/cm³; ṁ = 0.2568, 0.3744, and 0.5074 g/s; AoR ≈ 33.2–33.4° (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 8-10).

**DEM code and contact models.** Simulations used LIGGGHTS-Premium 4.X with Hertz–Mindlin normal/tangential contact mechanics and Coulomb friction. Rolling resistance was handled by the EPSD2 (elastic–plastic spring–dashpot) model with damping torque disabled. No cohesion model was applied because the powder was treated as non-cohesive. Particle size was coarse-grained sixfold following Bierwisch et al. (2009), and the timestep was kept below 20% of the Rayleigh critical timestep. CAD was done in SolidWorks, meshing in Gmsh, and post-processing in ParaView (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 5-6, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 5-6).

**Parameters varied and fixed.** Four factors were varied in a DoE: auger speed ω (400, 600, 800 rpm), particle–particle static friction μ_s,pp (0.3, 0.55, 0.8), particle–wall static friction μ_s,pw (0.1, 0.25, 0.4), and particle–particle rolling friction μ_r,pp (0.1, 0.4, 0.7). Fixed parameters included Young's moduli, Poisson ratios, restitution coefficients, particle density and scaled size, filling mass, gravity, and the numerical timestep (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 6-8).

**Design of experiments.** A quadratic D-optimal design required only 20 simulation runs (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 12-13, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 6-8).

**Regression models.** Separate quadratic multivariate response surfaces were fitted for AoR, BD, ṁ, and NA-TKE, with adjusted R² values of 0.975, 0.983, 0.998, and 0.986, respectively. Pareto charts and adjusted-response graphs ranked parameter effects (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 8-10).

**Contour-overlay calibration.** For each pair of calibration parameters (μ_r,pp and μ_s,pp), predicted contour plots of the three responses were superimposed. The experimental target values defined contour lines on each surface; their intersection dramatically narrowed the admissible region. Cornerstone optimization software then selected the minimum-error parameter combination. At 800 rpm the optimized combination used μ_s,pw = 0.347 as an optimized wall-friction value (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 10-12).

**Number of simulations.** Twenty DoE runs plus three confirmation runs (one at each speed) totaling 23 simulations (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 6-8, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 10-12).

**Validation.** Three confirmation DEM runs at 400, 600, and 800 rpm compared simulated AoR, BD, ṁ, and dosing time with experiments. Across 12 comparisons, the overall mean deviation was 0.87% and the maximum was 2.86% (for dosing time at 600 rpm) (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 12-13, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 10-12).

**Stated limitations.** The method was demonstrated only for one non-cohesive, free-flowing powder. The authors stated that future work should study more material properties and bulk behaviors and extend the method to cohesive powders (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 12-13). No held-out independent test types (shear cell, Hall flow, etc.) were used for validation; confirmation reused the same response types (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 10-12).

**Same-group lineage.** El Kassem et al.'s PAMM 2018 paper (doi:10.1002/pamm.201800261) was the first in this sequence, using DoE to calibrate angle of repose by varying rolling friction and restitution in auger-dosing DEM simulations (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 1-2). The CPM 2020 paper (doi:10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8) broadened the parametric study to six DEM inputs—including cohesion energy density via the modified SJKR model—and five macroscopic responses (AoR, porosity, mass flow rate, translational kinetic energy, computation time) for both free-flowing and cohesive powders (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 21-23, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 5-6, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2). The JDDST 2020 paper (doi:10.1016/j.jddst.2020.101950) applied multivariate statistics to analyze the impact of material attributes and process parameters on auger-dosing quality, complementing the DEM-calibration strand with an experimental/statistical quality perspective.

**DEM calibration methodology.** The contour-overlay approach for resolving parameter ambiguity was pioneered by Roessler et al. (2018, Powder Technology 343, 803–812, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2018.11.034), who showed that a single bulk response permits many DEM parameter combinations and that superimposing iso-response contours from multiple tests narrows the admissible region (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 10-12, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 13-14). Coetzee's 2017 review (Powder Technology 310, 104–142, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2017.01.015) provided the broader calibration framework (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 13-14). Wilkinson et al. (2017, Computers & Chemical Engineering 97, 161–174, doi:10.1016/j.compchemeng.2016.11.034) used statistical sensitivity analysis to link DEM inputs to Freeman-rheometer responses, providing precedent for the MVRA methodology (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 14-16).

**Screw-conveyor DEM.** Owen and Cleary (2009, Powder Technology 193, 274–288, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2009.03.012; 2010, Progress in CFD 10, 327–333) established DEM prediction of screw-conveyor throughput and power (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 13-14, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 14-16). Shimizu and Cundall (2001, J. Eng. Mech. 127, 864–872) provided early 3D DEM simulations of screw conveyors (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 13-14). Bierwisch et al. (2009, J. Mech. Phys. Solids 57, 10–31) introduced the coarse-graining method used for particle-size scaling (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 13-14).

## 4. Follow-Up by the Same Authors

Bilal El Kassem was a PhD candidate at Robert Bosch Packaging Technology GmbH in Stuttgart, supervised by Prof. Bernd Markert at the Institute of General Mechanics, RWTH Aachen University (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 14-16). The doctoral thesis is titled *"Machine design for auger dosing of powders by utilizing DEM simulations and analysis"* (RWTH Aachen University, 2021) and is explicitly cited by Kruppa et al. (2022) (kruppa2022increasingthedosing pages 1-11).

The publication sequence progressed as follows: (1) PAMM 2018 introduced auger-dosing DEM with DoE for AoR calibration; (2) JDDST 2020 (doi:10.1016/j.jddst.2020.101950) applied multivariate statistics to auger-dosing quality; (3) CPM 2020 (doi:10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8) extended the MVRA framework to cohesive powders using the SJKR cohesion model, examining six DEM inputs and five responses including porosity (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 21-23, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 5-6, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2); (4) KONA 2021 narrowed the method to a single-powder, multi-response auger calibration; and (5) the vertical loss-in-weight feeder prototype (doi:10.1080/10837450.2021.1901915) extended the device-design strand to gravimetric feeding.

The CPM 2020 paper is the most relevant extension to cohesive powders: it used SJKR cohesion energy density as a varied input alongside static and rolling friction, restitution, Young's modulus, and particle size, applied to angle-of-repose tests rather than to the auger-dosing setup itself (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 21-23, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 5-6). The doctoral thesis presumably consolidated these strands but was not accessible for full review.

No further publications by El Kassem, Salloum, Brinz, Heider, or Markert extending the auger-based DEM calibration to inverse identification, Bayesian inference, AM powders, or additional dosing devices were found in the retrieved literature.

### Three Closest Papers

1. **El Kassem et al., KONA 2021** — The single most directly comparable work: same concept of using an auger doser as a DEM calibration device with multiple bulk responses, LIGGGHTS Hertz–Mindlin contact, DoE, and regression-based identification. It differs from the user's work in orientation (vertical vs. inclinable), scope (one non-cohesive powder vs. 13 powders), calibration method (deterministic contour overlay vs. Bayesian inference), validation (self-consistent confirmation vs. held-out standard tests), and application domain (pharmaceutical vs. metal AM).

2. **El-Kassem et al., CPM 2020** — Extends the same group's approach to cohesive powders with SJKR cohesion energy density, six DEM inputs, and five responses. It demonstrates that the MVRA/DoE methodology can accommodate cohesion, but it uses angle-of-repose bench tests rather than auger-dosing responses, and it still produces point-estimate calibrations without uncertainty quantification.

3. **Sani et al., Progress in Additive Manufacturing 2026** — The closest work in the AM domain: calibrates DEM for Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V powders using surrogate models applied to rotating-drum responses with real particle-size distributions, geometry scaling, and two powders. It addresses AM spreadability motivation and uses a surrogate-based approach, but the calibration device is a rotating drum (not an auger), no Bayesian uncertainty is reported, and no held-out standard-test validation is performed.

### Novelty Claims to Make

The user's work can defensibly claim the following novelties relative to this citation network:

1. **A richer dosing-fingerprint excitation/response protocol** comprising speed-dependent mass-per-revolution at multiple tilt angles (0–30°), solenoid-tapped mass release, afterflow time constant, and zero-flow increment fraction — none of which appear in El Kassem or any retrieved citing work.

2. **Bayesian inference of effective powder properties from auger-dosing responses with posterior uncertainty**, as opposed to deterministic contour-overlay or optimization-based point estimates. While Bayesian DEM calibration exists (Cheng et al., GrainLearning), it has not been applied to an auger or screw-feeder response in the retrieved literature.

3. **Systematic fingerprinting of ≥13 chemically and morphologically diverse powders** on a single common device, spanning salts, food hydrocolloids, silicon, and gas-atomized metal alloy precursors, compared to El Kassem's single-powder demonstration.

4. **Held-out predictive validation** of doser-inferred effective properties against independent standardized tests (FT4 shear, Schulze ring shear, Hall/Carney flow, apparent/tap density, angle of repose, sieving, laser diffraction, loss on drying) — a validation design not found in any retrieved auger-DEM calibration study.

5. **Linkage from doser-inferred properties to AM spreadability and packing uniformity**, bridging the dosing-characterization and powder-bed-spreading literatures that currently operate in isolation.

6. **Integration into a self-driving laboratory** for alloy discovery, using an open-source, 3D-printed doser under closed-loop balance control with multi-task Bayesian optimization across powders.

### Claims to Drop or Soften

- **Do not claim** to be the first to use an auger doser as a DEM calibration device — El Kassem et al. (KONA 2021) explicitly proposed this (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 2-3).
- **Soften** any claim of first use of multiple bulk responses for DEM calibration — Roessler et al. (2018) and El Kassem et al. (2021) both demonstrated multi-response contour overlays (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 10-12, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 13-14).
- **Soften** any claim of first Bayesian DEM calibration — Cheng et al. (2018, 2024) established Bayesian DEM inference; the user's novelty is applying it to auger-dosing fingerprints for property inference.
- **Soften** any claim of first closed-loop powder dosing — Kruppa et al. (2022) demonstrated inline density-regulated screw dosing (kruppa2022increasingthedosing pages 1-11); the novelty is the specific open-source platform and the use of dosing dynamics as a mechanistic probe.
- **Do not claim** first DEM calibration for AM powders — Girnth et al. (2024), Sani et al. (2026), Meier et al. (2019), and others have parameterized DEM for AM feedstocks. The novelty is inferring AM-relevant properties from auger-dosing fingerprints and predicting spreadability from those inferred properties.
- **Soften** the claim of a parameter-free DEM prediction (105 mg/rev for salt) — specify all independently sourced inputs and clarify that this applies to one specific non-cohesive powder configuration; do not imply general parameter-free predictability.

In summary, the user's strongest novelty claim lies in the *combination* of (a) the enriched dosing-fingerprint protocol with tilt, tapping, afterflow, and intermittency responses, (b) Bayesian inverse inference with uncertainty quantification applied to that fingerprint, (c) systematic fingerprinting across a broad set of powders including metal AM feedstocks, (d) held-out validation against standard powder-characterization tests, and (e) downstream prediction of AM-relevant spreadability — none of which has been demonstrated as an integrated package in the existing auger-dosing DEM literature.

info.query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Our TMS 2027 abstract is titled 'Auger-Based Powder Dosing as a Mechanistic Probe of Powder Flow Behavior: Multi-Task Bayesian Calibration and Physics-Based Property Inference'. It frames calibration of the doser as multi-objective, multi-task Bayesian optimization of controller settings across powders (mostly alloy precursors and AM feedstocks such as AlSi10Mg and stainless steel, dosed under inert atmosphere), and DEM with cohesive-frictional contact laws and measured particle-size distributions to infer effective cohesion and friction from dosing data, checked against shear-cell and Hall-flow measurements, and to anticipate spreadability and packing uniformity. A web search for that title returned: B. El Kassem, N. Salloum, T. Brinz, Y. Heider and B. Markert, 'A Semi-Automated DEM Parameter Calibration Technique of Powders Based on Different Bulk Responses Extracted from Auger Dosing Experiments', KONA Powder and Particle Journal 38 (2021) 235-250, doi:10.14356/kona.2021010. Map the citation network of that paper. (1) Summarize exactly what it did: the dosing device and its geometry, the powders, the measured bulk responses, the DEM code and contact, rolling-resistance and cohesion models, which parameters were varied and which fixed, the design of experiments, the regression models, how the contour-overlay calibration works, how many simulations, how the result was validated and what limitations the authors state. (2) Backward: which earlier works does it build on most, including the same group's auger-dosing and DEM papers (for example PAMM 2018, Journal of Drug Delivery Science and Technology 2020, Computational Particle Mechanics 2020/2021) and the DEM calibration and screw-feeder literature it relies on? (3) Forward: list as many as possible of the papers that cite it (2021 to 2026), each with full reference and DOI, and for each say what it took from the KONA paper and whether it calibrates DEM from a feeder or doser response, uses surrogate-based or Bayesian inference with uncertainty, validates on tests held out of the fit (shear cell, Hall flow, angle of repose, tapped density), covers several powders, or concerns metal additive-manufacturing powders or spreading. Group the citing papers by theme. (4) Did the same authors follow it up (for example a doctoral thesis at RWTH Aachen, later Bosch or Aachen work) by extending the method to cohesive powders, other dosing devices, or inverse identification? (5) Compare with our work as described in the context: which of our elements already appear in El Kassem et al. or in the papers that cite it, and which do not (a tilt-angle sweep of an inclined auger, solenoid tapping, multi-task Bayesian optimization of dosing controller settings, a fingerprint over 13 or more powders, Bayesian inference with uncertainty, held-out shear-cell and Hall-flow checks, metal AM powders and spreadability). Name the three papers in this network closest to our work and state, as precisely as the evidence allows, what our novelty claim should be and which claims we should drop or soften.
